Multi-objective closed-loop charging scheduling strategy for electric vehicles based on user profiling and spatial–temporal mapping
Evaluation of modeling methods for lamellar phase change composites
From multi-physics modeling to AI-driven design: A cell-level comparative study and thermal-electrical collaborative optimization of H2- and NH3-fueled tubular SOFCs
Holistic planning and operational optimization of photovoltaic-driven district cooling systems with hybrid energy storage
A probabilistic evaluation of the evolution of capital costs and their reduction potential for new nuclear power plants
abstract: SUMMARYThis study presents a probabilistic evaluation of capital cost and construction schedule overruns and reduction potentials for building a series of new nuclear power plants in the United States. High capital costs for first-of-a-kind (FOAK) projects present a significant barrier to investments and creates a “first-mover” problem that can best be resolved through committed orderbook of several plants that are built sequentially. The study in this paper models the evolution of cost and construction duration in such orderbooks from the first to the last plant as a function of "levers" such as order book size, interest rates, design completion level before construction, etc. Results show that the first plant, which is assumed to be “first-of-a-kind”, is prone to significant cost and schedule overruns (median cost overrun of around 130%), while the last plant benefits from a gradual reduction in overruns as well as learning-based efficiencies that result in cost and schedule reductions (median cost reduction of around 30%).The study also identifies specific project characteristics of “levers” that determine overruns. For example, projects with FOAK capital cost overruns under 25% typically have at least five firm orders, 55% of their design completed before construction begins, a high level of design maturity, moderate to high proficiency in architecture/engineering and supply chain quality, a high proficiency in nuclear plant construction, and utilize modular civil construction. With the United States gearing up to significantly increase nuclear capacity, this study intends to provide insights into project planning aspects that enable the most economical pathways to achieve this scale up. The framework can be customized to any plant technology and has the potential to help policymakers, utilities, and stakeholders to make informed decisions by providing a detailed, customizable approach to cost estimation and reduction strategies.

title: A numerical approach to combined open gallery and porous flow in flooded mine workings
abstract: Mine water geothermal heating (MWGH) is increasingly recognised as a scalable, low-carbon heat source in former coalfields. Project viability, however, hinges on the hydraulics and heat exchange behaviour within complex networks, but also on realistic evaluation of heat pump performance. In this paper, we present an efficient numerical framework (GEMSToolbox) that couples steady-state pipe network hydraulics with semi-analytical heat exchange in both mine galleries and mined-out goaf zones, extended to include heat pump performance and pumping energy. This approach provides, for the first time, a full system evaluation tool dedicated to MWGH. A semi-analytical approach that efficiently represents 2-D porous flow in goaf zones enables rapid assessment of thermal evolution. We validate porous flow hydraulics and heat exchange against analytical benchmarks, and further compare model outputs with the well established software OpenGeoSys. This approach allows calculations that are an order of magnitude faster than conventional software tools, with temperature variation at the abstraction point of less than 4% over a 30-year period. A case study quantifies sensitivity to flow rate, injection and abstraction locations, porous zone properties, and pumping performance on a real mine system. The results highlight that the abstraction temperature is primarily controlled by flow rate and injection location, while pump efficiency strongly influences the system seasonal performance factor (SPF). This study reveals the value of GEMSToolbox in enabling large scale probabilistic site assessment which is not feasible with conventional software tools due to runtime constraints.

title: A distributed cooperative control method for hydraulic balance of central air conditioning based on dynamic compensation
Editorial Board
Effect of the surge motion on wake characteristics of a floating offshore wind turbine
abstract: Understanding how platform surge motion influences wake dynamics and downstream power availability of floating offshore wind turbines is essential for improving offshore wind energy efficiency. Previous studies have primarily focused on uniform inflow conditions, leaving the frequency-dependent wake behavior in a realistic atmospheric boundary layer unexplored. This study performs high-fidelity, GPU-accelerated large-eddy simulations of a NREL 5 MW reference turbine in an atmospheric boundary layer to investigate the effect of surge motion at different frequencies on wake dynamics. Results reveal a strong frequency dependence in velocity deficit, turbulence statistics, and coherent-structure dynamics. Within an effective reduced-frequency range (Strouhal number between 0.26 and 0.65), surge motion generates large-scale coherent structures that enhance momentum transport and accelerate wake recovery. An optimal frequency is identified at a Strouhal number of 0.39, at which the coherent structures achieve a favorable balance between spatial scale, persistence, and turbulent interaction, leading to the strongest wake recovery. At higher frequencies, the structures become smaller and more susceptible to turbulent dissipation, remaining confined near the rotor and contributing less effectively to downstream momentum transport. These results reveal a clear frequency-dependent mechanism by which surge motion modifies wake dynamics through its interaction with background ABL turbulence. These findings provide new physical insight into surge-induced wake dynamics in realistic ABL conditions and offer guidance for optimizing floating wind farm performance.

title: Design and implementation of a virtual islanding controller for renewable energy communities
abstract: The increasing penetration of Renewable Energy Sources (RES) in distribution networks calls for advanced flexibility services to support system operation. Among emerging solutions, Virtual Islanding (VI) has been proposed as a promising service; however, a dedicated control architecture enabling Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) to effectively provide VI has not yet been systematically addressed in the literature. This paper fills this gap by defining a novel control architecture specifically designed to coordinate the distributed resources of a REC during a VI request from the Distribution System Operator (DSO). The proposed coordinated two-level control framework combines a higher-level optimization-based energy management strategy, which schedules available flexibility resources over the VI time horizon, with a lower-level real-time controller that compensates for load and RES forecast deviations to ensure power balance. The proposed architecture is implemented and validated through detailed simulations on a representative REC providing the VI service in a 4.5-hour time window over a reference day. Results show the effectiveness of the proposed architecture, where the higher-level control provides suitable management of dispatchable resources while the FLL provides compensation for fast power variations. More quantitatively, a root-mean-square imbalance of 0.027 MW (0.28% of the total REC peak load), a maximum load imbalance of 0.224 MW (2.3% of the total REC peak load)) and an energy imbalance of 0.005 MWh (0.23% of the maximum RES shared energy of the considered test case) have been achieved in the proposed simulations, thereby ensuring effective real-time VI operation throughout the scheduled horizon. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility and effectiveness of RECs in providing VI as an innovative distributed flexibility service.

title: Coupled electromagnetic modelling to enhance the accuracy of thermoacoustic cooling system simulation
Environmental performance of solar photovoltaics across three generations: A cradle-to-gate comparison
abstract: • Harmonized cradle-to-gate environmental analysis of 8 PV panels across 3 generations. • Process energy and structural materials drive >50% of PV global warming impact. • 2nd-generation is more sustainable but limited deployment (<5%) by cost-efficiency. • Tandem panels offer ∼30% lower environmental impact over all categories. • Energy payback time (EPBT) varied from 0.1 to 1.1 years across all PV technologies. Solar photovoltaic (PV) systems are essential for low-carbon electricity generation. This study addresses current critical gap in comparative life-cycle data by conducting a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) of eight representative PV panels across three generations. By adopting a harmonized methodological framework, the analysis overcomes inconsistencies that hindered comparisons across prior studies, enabling robust cross generation benchmarking. Results identify that technological advances in first-generation solar PV panels have driven a consistent decline in environmental impacts across all six evaluated categories. Emerging third-generation technologies show improved environmental performance over established first-generation systems. This LCA modelling indicates a marked reduction in global warming (GW) impacts for first-generation PV panels, decreasing from 30 to below 25 g CO 2 eq/kWh, primarily driven by improvements in conversion efficiency. Second-generation technologies achieve the lowest GW impacts (< 20 g CO 2 eq/kWh), although their widespread deployment remains constrained by cost-effectiveness limitations. Contribution analysis shows that embodied energy in manufacturing and aluminum alloy used in encapsulation accounted for 30.6-41.7% and 10.5-26.9% of the total impacts, respectively, highlighting the dependence on non-renewable energy sources. Encapsulation emerges as a major contributor to mineral resource scarcity, while the use of chalcogenide compounds in second-generation absorber layers further exacerbates this impact. Sensitivity analysis shows that emerging tandem technologies must achieve operational lifetimes exceeding 15-year and reduce annual degradation rate below 2% to deliver a sustainability advantage over silicon-based modules. Overall, these findings provide actionable insights to guide sustainable PV manufacturing strategies and inform evidence-based decisions on future solar energy deployment.

title: Resilience of collaborative microgrids towards volatility: Seasonal effects, demand fluctuations, and weather variations
abstract: • Power volatility absorption of collaborative MGs is investigated. • Resilience of pre-contracted grid order update strategy against seasons is verified. • Real-time simulations study demand and weather effects on the proposed strategy. • Collaborative microgrids outperform selfish ones in extreme weather events. One of the primary issues experienced by contemporary energy systems is the volatility and uncertainty of weather conditions. Conventional energy systems depend on unsustainable sources such as coal or gas to cope with the uncertainty of demand. Energy systems relying on renewables such as wind and solar face the same demand uncertainty but also have to cope with the variability of weather. Handling this double-sided variability is a critical challenge of modern energy systems. This research evaluates the power volatility absorption from utility grids by collaborative microgrids (MGs), by using a pre-contracted order updates (COU) operational strategy at the MG level. This strategy distinguishes the collaborative MG employing the COU strategy from the selfish MG utilizing the conventional spot order update strategy. The purpose of this research is to investigate how real-world uncertainties, such as forecasting errors and demand fluctuations impact the collaborative MG system. The resilience and robustness of the COU approach were assessed against weather and demand fluctuations. Seasonal effect was analysed to determine the optimal COU scenario across seasons. The results indicate that the COU strategy, particularly the planned volatile demand scenario, demonstrates adaptability to all seasonal fluctuations, reducing the unplanned volatile demand by 87% compared to selfish MG during the most volatile season (Winter). In the context of extreme weather events, especially in the absence of wind, the collaborative MG diminished the unplanned volatile demand by 93% in contrast to the selfish MG.

title: Robust low-carbon planning of regional integrated energy systems with cross-seasonal hydrogen shifting and biogenic carbon recycling
Integrated techno-economic assessment of heating electrification and decarbonization pathways in a remote First Nation microgrid
abstract: Energy insecurity persists in many remote Indigenous communities in Northern Canada, where electricity is commonly supplied by diesel microgrids and space heating relies on imported fuels such as propane, resulting in high operating costs, logistical vulnerability, and greenhouse gas emissions. This study evaluates integrated pathways to improve energy security and reduce operational emissions in Gull Bay First Nation (Kiashke Zaaging Anishinaabek), a remote Ojibwe community in Northern Ontario served by an islanded photovoltaic–battery–diesel microgrid. Using measured microgrid and weather data combined with building energy simulations implemented through the TOOLS4Cities platform, three scenarios are assessed: (i) the current baseline system with propane- and wood-based heating, (ii) full heating electrification using air-source heat pumps coupled with photovoltaics and battery energy storage system expansion optimized via non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II, and (iii) conversion to biomass boilers. The biomass scenario reduces total operational emissions by 19% relative to the baseline and decreases heating-related emissions by 75%, with an estimated discounted payback period of 11 years. Full heating electrification achieves the largest emissions reduction (approximately 48%) but requires substantial expansion of photovoltaic-storage systems and a high upfront investment in an islanded system, with discounted payback periods near 10 years under baseline fuel prices. Sensitivity analysis indicates that escalating fuel prices improve the payback of both electrification and biomass pathways. The study contributes an integrated system-level framework linking heating transitions with islanded microgrid dispatch constraints and photovoltaic–battery expansion planning, benchmarked against measured microgrid data to identify operational limitations often overlooked in purely simulation-based studies.

title: Biomass potential and effect of European Union regulation on non-productive areas and fallow land - a case study of the Czech Republic
Energy, environmental, and economic assessment of sustainable fuels from wet biomass via hydrothermal, sorbent-enhanced gasification, and Fischer-Tropsch route
From case-specific to general tuning: A structured, system-level framework for scalable RCCI simulation
abstract: Multi-zone models (MZMs) are widely used for system-level simulation of reactivity-controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines. However, their predictive robustness remains strongly dependent on CFD-informed fuel stratification inputs, case-specific calibration and fuel-dependent chemical kinetic mechanisms. This limits their transferability across engine platforms and operating conditions. This study addresses these limitations by developing a structured, CFD-independent reduced-order predictive framework for scalable engine-level RCCI simulation. Implemented within the University of Vaasa’s advanced thermo-kinetic multi-zone model (UVATZ), the methodology integrates (i) systematic reactivity scaling to compensate for chemical kinetic deficiencies without disturbing thermodynamic boundary conditions, and (ii) a generalised beta-distribution-based high-reactivity fuel stratification model which eliminates reliance on CFD-derived mixture profiles. The framework is encapsulated in a modular solver architecture and uses a structured calibration procedure requiring only limited test-bench data to achieve predictive capability. The new submodels were assessed for scalability across different chemical kinetic mechanisms, and their physical consistency was verified against CFD spray simulations. The complete framework was experimentally validated using 40 operating points from a prototype Wärtsilä W31 medium-speed dual-fuel engine operating in RCCI mode. All performance metrics were predicted within ±6%, without case-specific tuning. CA50 errors were below 5 CAD (±1 CAD standard deviation). Model deviations remained within measured cycle-to-cycle variability, and simulation time did not exceed three minutes per cycle, comparing favourably against best-in-class multi-zone models which rely on calibration to a specific operating point.

title: Energy, exergy, economic, environmental, and eco-efficiency assessment of renewable-driven electrochemical methanol and ammonia production integrated with autothermal biogas reforming
abstract: This study assesses the feasibility of renewable-driven electrochemical methanol and ammonia production integrated with biogas-based autothermal reforming (ATR). Five system configurations, such as scenarios A, B, C, D, and E, which combine ATR, the water–gas shift reaction, and electrochemical reduction of CO2 and nitrogen powered by wind energy, are evaluated using analyses of energy, exergy, economics, environment, and eco-efficiency. Results show that electrochemical units dominate electricity consumption and capital cost, while methanol synthesis enables up to 40–50% CO2 emission reduction through carbon utilization. Exergy-based indicators reveal that integrated product systems achieve higher sustainability performance, whereas hydrogen-only configurations show lower environmental benefits. Economic results indicate payback periods between 4.8 and 8.5 years, with competitive hydrogen costs but higher methanol and ammonia production costs. Scenarios E and D have the lowest hydrogen production costs at 3.364 and 3.591 €/kg, respectively. Scenarios B and A have the highest costs, at 11.233 and 9.491 €/kg, respectively. However, Scenario C is competitive and profitable at 5.347 €/kg. The cost of producing methanol ranges from 1342.285 to 2030.436 €/tonne, while the cost of producing ammonia ranges from 1165.723 to 2211.509 €/tonne. The cost of producing oxygen and nitrogen is well above market levels, ranging from 793.089 to 1130.549 €/tonne for oxygen and from 249.449 to 881.778 €/tonne for nitrogen. Overall, the findings demonstrate that integrated renewable-driven ATR systems are technically viable, with future competitiveness strongly dependent on advances in electrochemical cell efficiency and cost reduction.

title: Investigation of pressure fluctuations induced by impeller blockage in high-speed miniature cooling pumps for electric vehicle thermal management systems
Experimental performance and exergy analysis of a net-zero energy heat pump drying system integrated with photovoltaics and carbon fiber film heaters

Triply periodic minimal surface supported Pt-catalyst for enhanced low-carbon micro power systems

Experimental investigation on the thermal performance of a 28-kWh novel packed-bed cryogenic energy storage platform
Comparative performance evaluation of sensible and latent thermal energy storage media integrated into a solar dryer using classical and advanced exergoeconomic and exergy analyses
Techno-enviro-economic analysis of solid oxide electrolysis cell architectures
abstract: Solid oxide electrolysers (SOE) are able to produce hydrogen, an important building block in decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors, with class-leading efficiencies. However, scaling up SOE technology remains challenging due to high costs and short lifetimes, which differ among the different SOE cell architectures. This work compares and contrasts the economic and environmental impact of scaling up different SOE cell architectures to a 1MW stack module. A parallelized and experimentally validated model was used to optimize each architecture across a broad range of material and microstructure combinations. Among the evaluated architectures, the anode-supported architecture achieved the highest current density, however, its high degradation rate currently makes it the least viable option. It must address the degradation, even if it is achieved by decreasing current density. The metal-supported architecture stands out as the cheapest architecture, but due to the low current densities and thus, increased material demand to manufacture the comparatively larger stack modules, its geopolitical supply chain risk is high. It requires stabler and more heat-resistant stainless steel to limit degradation and operate at 650 °C to decrease stack size and material supply chain risk by 20%. Remarkably, the electrolyte supported architecture using a 150 µm 1Ce10SSZ electrolyte is the most favourable at 103 ton CO 2 emissions, 254 € of material supply chain risk and 0.42M$ stack costs. Its stability and low geopolitical supply chain risk perhaps warrant a renewed focus on the electrolyte-supported architecture. • A large parametric sweep over millions of different microstructures in the quest for optimal solid oxide electrolysis architectures. • The three solid oxide electrolysis architectures are compared on costs, CO 2 emissions from manufacturing and the critical material supply risk disruption for 1MW stack modules. • Electrolyte supported solid oxide cell with a 150 μ m 1Ce10SSZ electrolyte after 4 years of operation, shows the lowest impact over all three categories. • Possible improvements in microstructure design and operation strategies are outlined for each of the architectures in reducing costs, CO 2 emissions from manufacturing and the critical material supply risk disruption.

title: Experimental performance analysis of a forward and backward bent ducts for wave energy harvesting and attenuation
Development of a hierarchical control strategy integrating future load prediction and NMPC for residential hybrid PEMFC-CHP systems
Study on control strategy optimization and performance analysis of a PV/T-coupled transcritical CO2 heat pump system with ejector and vapor injection based on environmental mode switching
abstract: PV/T (photovoltaic/thermal) coupled heat pump systems improve energy efficiency through the cascaded utilisation of solar energy in a "light-to-electricity-to-heat" conversion process, positioning them as a promising integrated energy utilisation technology. This paper integrates an ejector and vapor injection technique into a PV/T dual-source transcritical CO2 heat pump system and proposes a multi-mode switching PV/T-coupled injection-enhanced transcritical CO2 heat pump system (PV/T-EIHP) to enhance system performance under low ambient temperature conditions. A thermodynamic simulation model incorporating a thermal storage tank was developed. The model was refined through the fitting of optimal high-pressure side pressure formulas under various operating modes. System control strategy optimisation was conducted by comparing performance across all operating modes under low ambient temperature conditions, followed by simulations of the system's operational characteristics on a typical winter day. The results indicate that adopting a control strategy that switches to the Sole Ejector Mode (SEJM) when the evaporation temperature is ≥5 °C and employs Ejector Vapor Injection Mode (EVIM) during the remaining periods improves the COP of the PV/T-EIHP system by 5.32% to 14.03% relative to the PV/T-DSHP system. Under typical sunny and overcast winter conditions in Luntai, Xinjiang, the system achieved daily average COPs of 3.25 and 2.33, respectively. On sunny days, the PV/T system exhibited a daily average comprehensive conversion efficiency of 35.49%, with solar power generation covering 63.48% of the electricity demand during irradiation hours. This study provides a theoretical foundation for the optimised design and operational control of PV/T dual-source transcritical CO2 heat pump systems.

title: Sustainable water and energy for water-stressed coastal cities under future climate scenarios
abstract: The Impact of climate change on solar-thermal power and desalination infrastructure was evaluated for 23 water-stressed coastal cities using projections from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) for both moderate and high emission scenarios through to 2099. Using costs as a proxy measure of impact, the study assessed future changes in solar radiation, temperature, wind speed, seawater temperature, and salinity, combined with multi-criteria geospatial screening to identify suitable coastal sites, and applied a techno-economic model with SAM and a numerical MED framework. The results indicate that cities such as Beirut, Biobío, and Valparaíso show significant improvements in future feasibility, with projected increases in solar radiation of up to 9.9%, resulting in levelized cost of electricity reductions of over 1.2 USD¢/kWh. In contrast, cities like Aden and Dubai face declines in DNI of up to 4.2%, with corresponding ∼ 6% increases in levelized cost of electricity, highlighting the investment risk under high-emission scenarios. In all climate scenarios/locations, solar thermal desalination system was demonstrated as a sustainable source of electricity and water with high carbon reduction potential. For example, in Jeddah under the SSP2-4.5 near-future scenario, deploying a system with an annual desalination capacity of 3.28 × 10⁶ m 3 results in 1.72 tonnes of CO 2 emissions per year, compared to 6,630 tonnes and 20,800 tonnes annually for conventional reverse osmosis membrane and multi-effect distillation systems, respectively. Overall, it is critical to consider the effect of future climates on the feasibility of solar driven thermal desalination to unlock solar electricity and freshwater for densely populated coastal cities.

title: Design and experimental analysis for waste heat power generation system from aluminum reduction cell’s sidewalls

Integration of ammonia-fueled protonic ceramic fuel cells with non-uniform thermoelectric generators: Performance evaluation and optimization

Dynamic model of parachute-based airborne wind energy system in steady wind field
Comparative study of solar-assisted chemical looping steam and dry gasification systems in direct reduced iron production
abstract: The iron and steel industry is one of the most difficult industrial sectors to decarbonize, and the carbon performance of direct reduced iron (DRI) production depends strongly on the sources of reducing gas and high-temperature process heat. However, the effects of different gasifying environments on syngas quality and system-level performance remain insufficiently understood for integrated solar-assisted biomass chemical looping DRI systems. This study hypothesizes that concentrated solar heat can reduce combustion-derived heat demand, while steam and carbon dioxide can be used to regulate the H 2 /CO ratio for shaft-furnace-compatible operation. To test this, an Aspen Plus-based integrated process model was established and applied to compare steam-only, CO 2 -only, and mixed steam/CO 2 configurations using sensitivity, thermodynamic, environmental, and techno-economic analyses. All three cases achieved DRI-compatible performance, with metallization levels of 90.50–92.88%, near-autothermal fuel-reactor operation at 7.01–7.34 MW solar heat input, and an annual operating time of approximately 8,100 h under the selected solar multiple and thermal storage design. The mixed steam/CO 2 case showed the most balanced overall performance, giving the lowest specific exergy consumption (8793.4 kJ/kg-DRI), the lowest greenhouse-gas intensity (296.43 kg CO 2 -eq/t-DRI), and the lowest levelized DRI cost without carbon credit (338.07 USD/t-DRI). These results indicate that solar-assisted biomass chemical looping is a technically feasible pathway for low-carbon DRI production, and that the mixed gasification strategy provides the best compromise among thermodynamic performance, environmental benefits, and baseline economic competitiveness.

title: Development of a green hydrogen waste heat utilization system and supply–demand analysis: Considering fluctuation and uncertainty
Design and management of multi-energy system including power-to-heat thermal storage for assessment of economic and environmental performances
Improving the performance of a hexagonal thermoelectric generator by utilizing narrow regions with heat pipes
Ensuring reliability in 100% renewable microgrids: A scenario-based joint planning and operational design framework
abstract: Off-grid microgrids powered entirely by renewable energy sources face substantial challenges in achieving utility-grade reliability standards. Existing microgrid planning frameworks often prioritize cost minimization while treating reliability as a secondary metric, thereby leading to suboptimal designs. This paper presents a comprehensive scenario-based optimization framework that simultaneously addresses long-term capacity planning and short-term operational dispatch in two stages for 100%-renewable microgrids. The developed two-stage stochastic programming model co-optimizes the investment and operation of photovoltaic generation and battery energy storage, while ensuring compliance with stringent reliability constraints following utility grid standards. Network modeling with operational constraints, such as line capacities and voltage limits, is incorporated to allow distributed resource placement leveraging power sharing between microgrid nodes. A novel scenario generation approach captures critical uncertainties, including seasonal demand fluctuations, solar output variations, and probabilistic equipment failures, through the statistical clustering of historical data. The optimization framework integrates utility-grade reliability constraints limiting the expected energy not served to below 0.002% of the annual demand while minimizing the total system costs. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving 99.998% supply reliability using only photovoltaic power and battery energy storage. The optimized network-aware distributed resource allocation provides inherent resilience through power rerouting during component outages, maintaining load continuity even under simultaneous equipment failures. This study confirms the feasibility of 100%-renewable microgrids to support remote communities while meeting utility-grade reliability benchmarks.

title: Experimental and modeling analysis of a novel discontinuous fins PCHE with coupled variable compactness and thermal resistance rebalancing strategy
Physics-informed hybrid Digital Twin for decoupling multi-source degradation in marine propulsion systems
Editorial Board
Hydrogen from single-layer and multi-layer plastic films via nonthermal plasma
abstract: The treatment of plastic waste poses significant societal challenges, as mismanaged waste can harm human health and ecological systems. However, plastic waste represents a feedstock rich in hydrogen - an essential energy carrier for a carbon-neutral future. Plasma technology provides a compelling route for plastic waste valorization through the direct use of electricity, potentially with no pressurization, solvents, catalysts, or CO2 emissions. In this work, we investigate atmospheric pressure streamer dielectric-barrier discharge (sDBD) plasma for hydrogen production from representative plastic films. We examine the effects of dielectric barrier properties, feedstock morphology, polymer chemical structure, and multi-layer film architecture. Plasma treatment of low-density polyethylene (LDPE) in powder and film forms, as well as from three single-layer films (LDPE, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), and nylon 6,6) and two aluminum-containing multi-layer films are analyzed via chemical, electrical, optical, and spectroscopic diagnostics together with complementary models describing electrical dynamics, thermal-electrical energy coupling, and polymer decomposition. LDPE powder yields more than twice the hydrogen from LDPE film due to greater plasma – feedstock interaction. PET and nylon 6,6 films also exhibit more than double the hydrogen recovery of LDPE film, attributable to their chemical and structural properties. The aluminum layer in the multi-layer films diverts plasma away from the polymers, leading to the lowest hydrogen yields. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of nonthermal plasma for hydrogen production from plastic films.​

title: Building-integrated falling-film night cooling coupled with photovoltaic panels: full-scale evaluation of cooling potential at the Cartuja Qanat Urban-Lab
Influence of buoyancy effects on supercritical pressure carbon dioxide convective heat transfer in triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) channels
A water-cooled concentrating bifacial photovoltaic/thermal system: Performance evaluation considering the trade-off between panel’s optical losses and system’s thermal-electrical gains
Meta-reinforcement learning for multi-energy building microgrids: Curriculum design, rapid adaptation, and scalable deployment
abstract: Multi-energy building microgrids meeting local demands is a promising solution for sustainable and self-sufficient energy communities. However, consumption diversity across heterogeneous buildings creates a deployment bottleneck that requires an adaptive and scalable energy-management strategy. A novel meta-reinforcement learning framework was proposed in this study that integrates an enhanced reptile-based meta-learning algorithm with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to learn a generalized policy capable of rapid building-specific personalization. Two curriculum learning approaches were applied to assess the impact of task organization on meta-learning outcomes, focusing on seasonal variations and building diversity. Rigorous hyperparameter optimization was performed to identify high-performance models (three per curriculum) for comprehensive deployment analysis. The trained meta-policies were deployed on five unseen test buildings across four seasons. The adapted policies achieved a mean reward improvement of 23.9% over the trained meta-policy, with constraint violations reducing by 38% and daily operating costs decreasing by 12.2%, statistically validated through a Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p = 1.11 × 10 − 20 ). Curriculum-2 (progressive building diversity) outperformed Curriculum-1 (seasonal progression) by 53% in mean adaptation improvement, demonstrating that learning building heterogeneity is more valuable than mastering seasonal patterns for adaptive energy management. Future research directions include hardware-in-the-loop validation, adaptive curricula, and multi-agent coordination for community-scale deployment.

title: Experimental investigation of a cryogenic-enhanced ORC for battery and fuel-cell waste-heat recovery in marine hybrid propulsion
Working towards accomplishing SDG 7 in Australia with an effective home energy management system
abstract: The global energy landscape is undergoing transformation to mitigate climate change and fulfil Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7), which targets affordable, reliable, sustainable, and universally accessible modern energy. Despite extensive adoption of residential photovoltaic (PV) systems in Australia, several practical challenges remain, including high electricity costs, low self-consumption of PV generation, and energy accessibility for the remote regions and First Nations communities. This study proposes a home energy management system (HEMS) incorporating the reinforcement learning (RL)-based model to dynamically manage energy flows among residential PV generation, battery storage systems, household loads, and the grid. The energy scheduling problem is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and solved using a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent that learns optimal dispatch strategies under dynamic operating conditions. The reward function integrates electricity cost, self-consumption ratio (SCR), and grid dependency (GD). A multi-objective search based on the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) is employed to determine suitable combinations of reward weights. To better represent real residential operation, the model further incorporates battery degradation and grid outage scenarios into the system simulation. Simulation results based on realistic Australian residential load profiles and tariff structures demonstrate satisfactory operational performance. The results demonstrate that the proposed HEMS can adapt to households with different PV generation and demand patterns while coordinating PV–battery operation to improve the utilization of locally generated solar energy and reduce reliance on grid electricity. The analysis highlights the trade-off between battery utilization and long-term degradation, as well as the potential of PV–battery systems to improve household energy resilience during grid outage events. In addressing the practical implementation of SDG 7 within the Australian context, the proposed HEMS offers critical policy, social, and economic implications. The system enhances affordability by significantly reducing household electricity bills and shortening investment payback periods, supports sustainability by increasing local renewable energy utilization, and improves energy accessibility by supporting stable and cost-effective electricity for remote and underserved communities. Policy recommendations are included to suggest stable incentives for battery storage and solar feed-in tariffs, promote integrated HEMS solutions, and advance equitable energy access.

title: Optimization of serrated finned plate exhaust heat exchangers under all operating conditions considering soot deposition
Modeling and performance assessment of Concentrated Photovoltaic Thermal solar tower systems
abstract: Concentrated Photovoltaic Thermal (CPVT) solar towers combine high efficiency Photovoltaic (PV) and Concentrated Solar Thermal (CST) technologies to simultaneously generate electricity and recover heat from the cooling system. Integration of thermal energy storage (TES) provides flexibility, reducing curtailment and dependence on solar availability. Literature on CPVT towers lacks integrated receiver and plant models with techno-economic analyses, and their thermo-electric performance under solar tower-specific conditions is poorly characterized. This work develops a comprehensive CPVT solar tower model accounting for environmental factors such as soiling and flux non-uniformities from heliostat field-generated maps. A thermo-electrical receiver model is coupled with TES and power block to calculate annual energy yield, levelized and actual cost of electricity (LCOE, ACOE). The model is demonstrated through a case study in Australia. Receiver connections are optimized to minimize mismatches, resulting in a residual efficiency loss of 5.7%. Performance is minimally affected by sun position, with across- and intra-day efficiency variations of 0.6–2.2%. The plant is analyzed under two dispatch scenarios: continuous, producing 11.08 GW h yr -1 with LCOE of 83.09 $/MWh; and grid-constrained, reducing yield by 30% and resulting in ACOE of 119.74 $/MWh. The CPVT plant demonstrates economic competitiveness with Concentrated Solar Power (CSP), yet remains less competitive than PV, while exhibiting greater operational flexibility and lower curtailment. Overall, the developed model establishes a techno-economic framework for evaluating CPVT solar towers within the broader solar energy landscape, demonstrating avenues for competitive dispatchability and further performance improvement.

title: Physics-Informed neural networks with resnet-based two-stage training for transient multi-domain wellbore temperature prediction in deep drilling
Forecast-informed daily energy dispatch for cost and emission reduction: Evidence from an emerging economy power system
Sediment characterization and machine learning-based turbine abrasion risk assessment for Modi Khola hydropower plant, Nepal
Simultaneous design and operation of integrated thermal energy systems via disjunctive multi-period nonlinear optimization
Carbonate gradient reverse electrodialysis (CG–RED) enabled by bipolar membrane–induced pH–swing
abstract: Reverse electrodialysis (RED) is a promising technology for harvesting salinity–gradient energy; however, its performance is fundamentally constrained by the limited ionic concentration differences available in natural water sources. Here, we propose a carbonate gradient reverse electrodialysis (CG–RED) system in which the conventional NaCl salinity gradient is coupled with pH–dependent carbonate speciation. Carbonate speciation is actively regulated using a bipolar membrane (BPM)–induced pH–swing, generated via water dissociation under reverse bias. This pH modulation alters the relative distribution of carbonate species, thereby modifying the effective Nernstian driving force through redistribution of ionic contributions within the membrane system. Under representative operating conditions, the CG–RED system exhibits changes in open circuit voltage and power density compared to conventional NaCl–based RED, reflecting the combined effects of carbonate addition and pH–dependent speciation control. The contribution of the pH–swing itself results in a modest incremental change in power output under otherwise identical electrolyte conditions. Importantly, the present system does not achieve net-positive energy output, as the electrical energy required for the BPM–driven pH–swing exceeds the incremental gain in CG–RED performance under the current configuration. Therefore, this work is intended to provide mechanistic insight into the coupling between carbonate equilibrium, pH modulation, and ion transport in multi-ionic RED systems, rather than to demonstrate an energetically optimized power generation device. These findings establish pH–driven speciation control as an additional electrochemical degree of freedom for modulating ion transport behavior in salinity gradient systems.

title: Performance and uniformity enhancement in low‑platinum PEMFCs via synergistic dual‑segment power‑law platinum and ionomer gradients: A physics‑informed multi‑objective optimization approach
A collaborative treatment strategy for anaerobic digestion byproducts of food waste: Steam co-gasification of digestate and waste plastic
Hydrogen production via a novel CoO/Co based chemical looping water gas shift: Validation and improvement strategies
abstract: Hydrogen production via thermochemical cycles represents an attractive, simple, and clean pathway for hydrogen generation. In this work, a novel chemical looping water gas shift (CL-WGS) process for hydrogen production using CoO as oxygen carrier and CO as reducing agent was developed and validated. The process exhibited high hydrogen production capacity and excellent reversibility achieving a total hydrogen production of 12.72 mmol H 2 /g material over ten redox cycles. Hydrogen production increased upon cycling from 0.89 mmol H 2 /g material in the first cycle to 1.61 mmol H 2 /g material in the tenth cycle. This enhanced hydrogen production is attributed to a higher accessible active surface area upon cycling. Carbon deposition played a key role in this enhancement, acting as a physical spacer and promoting particle fragmentation upon extended cycling. Further improvements in hydrogen production were achieved via partial substitution of CoO with 10 mol% NiO and the addition of 5 wt% TiO 2 nanoparticles, both of which enhanced CoO reducibility and mitigated particle sintering. The highest performance was obtained for the thermochemical material containing both NiO and TiO 2 , yielding 24.81 mmol H 2 /g material over ten redox cycles and highlighting the synergistic effect between the two strategies.

title: Time-varying aerodynamic damping of offshore wind turbines: An analytical formulation
abstract: A 15-degree-of-freedom aero-servo-elastic system model incorporating various wind turbine conditions and wind-field features is developed using a modal-based multibody formulation. The effective wind velocity and associated quantities are decomposed into time-varying steady and incremental components, allowing analytical derivation of the aerodynamic damping and stiffness matrices for rapid evaluation of time-varying aerodynamic damping ratios (ADRs) via instantaneous complex-eigenvalue analysis. The results show that the mean ADRs exhibit multi-stage wind-speed dependence under operational scenarios due to servo controls, but tend to be quasi-linear under idling scenarios. Wind shear and veer alone noticeably affect the mean ADRs of only a few aeroelastic modes, such as the rotor edgewise whirling modes. In contrast to operational scenarios, under idling scenarios the combined effects of the three wind-field features — primarily governed by yaw misalignment — are generally much stronger, with wind veer assuming a prominent role. More non-ideal inflow and higher wind speeds amplify 3 P-dominated time-varying ADR behavior, which is particularly critical for lightly damped aeroelastic modes. Under the combined effects, pronounced temporal variability drives the rotor second and third edgewise whirling modes of the idling system into periodically negative ADRs, even at yaw misalignments below 10°. With further increases in yaw misalignment, negative ADRs become more pronounced, extending over broader and even entire wind-speed ranges and across an increasing number of aeroelastic modes, thereby reflecting an enhanced risk of multi-modal aeroelastic instability.

Design and performance study for a non-tracking concentrator solar brackish water evaporating device with lotus petal-inspired structure
Energy circuit theory-enabled quasi-dynamic security assessment for integrated electricity-gas energy system
Synergistic integration of waste heat and solar energy in a hybrid adsorption chiller-vapor compression heat pump system for large-scale greenhouse cooling
Enhancing renewable energy performance of biogas systems through Sargassum co-digestion and methane recovery: An integrated life cycle assessment
A novel ammonia production system based on Co‑gasification of coal and biomass

Solar daylighting to offset LED lighting in vertical Farming: A Techno-Economic study of light pipes
abstract: Vertical farming is a controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) approach in which crops are grown in stacked layers under regulated climate and lighting, enabling predictable production but requiring high electricity input. This study quantifies the techno-economic impact of roof-mounted daylighting in a three-tier container vertical farm using a light-pipe (LP) system that delivers sunlight to the upper tier. The optical chain, comprising a straight duct and a tilting aluminum-coated mirror within a rotating dome, was modelled in Tonatiuh to estimate crop-level photon delivery and solar gains. These outputs were coupled with a transient AGRI-Energy model to perform year-round simulations for Dubai. Tier-3 strategies were compared against a fully LED benchmark, including daylight-only operation, on/off supplementation, PWM dimming, UV-IR filtering, variable-transmittance control, and simple glazing. Ray-tracing predicted an overall LP optical efficiency of 45%-75%, depending on solar position, quantifying the fraction of incident daylight at the collector aperture delivered to the target growing zone. Daylight-only operation reduced the total three-tier yield by 17% and was not economically viable despite 27-29% electricity savings. Hybrid daylight-LED strategies preserved benchmark yield while reducing electricity use. PWM dimming combined with UV-IR filtering achieved the lowest specific electricity energy consumption (6.32 kWh/kg), 14% below the benchmark. Overall, viability remains CAPEX-limited because achievable electricity savings are insufficient to offset the added investment and thus improves mainly under high electricity and carbon-price contexts, although the LP system delivers a 15-38% lower light cost than an optical-fiber reference under identical incident daylight.

title: Comparative techno-economic analysis of alcohol-to-jet pathways from ethanol and mixed alcohols, within an integrated sugarcane biorefinery
abstract: Alcohol-to-jet (AtJ) processing represents a promising yet cost-prohibitive pathway for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production. This work develops a process-level techno-economic evaluation of six novel AtJ configurations within an integrated sugarcane biorefinery, explicitly incorporating commercial dehydration technologies and energy self-sufficient operation. Hydrous and anhydrous ethanol pathways yielded similar minimum aviation fuel selling prices (MAFSP) (3.68 US$/L), as upstream energy savings were offset by downstream penalties. High-pressure dehydration (Hummingbird®-type) reduced MAFSP to 3.63 US$/L and CAPEX by 12% (237 vs 269 million US$) relative to low-pressure dehydration (Atol®-type), demonstrating it as a preferred design basis to minimise energy consumption and capital intensity. Inclusion of C 8 hydrocarbons within the kerosene pool reduced MAFSP by 55%, but blending constraints (<10%) limit practical deployment. Upgrading C 8 to jet-range aromatics reduced MAFSP by 17% while enabling drop-in fuel compatibility, positioning aromatics production as a fuel quality and cost optimisation strategy. Mixed alcohol pathways exhibited marginally higher MAFSPs (3.76 US$/L) due to capital-intensive ethanol coupling highlighting upstream alcohol production as a priority research area for achieving cost-competitive AtJ fuels. These results demonstrate key design trade-offs across feedstock choice, dehydration technologies and product upgrading, identifying actionable levers for technology selection and process optimisation in AtJ deployment.

Dynamic analysis of a novel liquid carbon dioxide system for electric energy storage
abstract: The rapid expansion of intermittent renewable energy sources and the progressive electrification of end-use sectors require high-efficiency and flexible large-scale electrical energy storage solutions. Existing liquid carbon dioxide (LCO 2 ) energy storage systems are often limited by simplified thermodynamic modeling and suboptimal cycle configurations that include throttling losses and inadequate thermal management. This work hypothesizes that a throttling-free LCO 2 configuration integrating two-stage intercooling, comprehensive waste heat recovery, and a power-to-cool strategy for density enhancement can significantly improve round-trip efficiency and operational flexibility under realistic dynamic conditions. To test this hypothesis, a high-fidelity dynamic real-gas model was developed within a TRNSYS–MATLAB co-simulation framework and applied to a residential district equipped with a 5.02 MW photovoltaic field and a 3.00 MW evacuated solar collector field, explicitly incorporating intercooling, elimination of throttling processes, and a multi-module power-to-cool system to reduce liquid CO 2 temperature before storage. The results show that the proposed system achieves a net round-trip efficiency of 72.5%, recovers 63.0% of compression waste heat, supplies approximately 19.0% of the annual electrical demand through stored CO 2 , and reduces grid electricity consumption by about 62.3%. These findings demonstrate that the combined adoption of intercooling, throttling elimination, and density-boosting power-to-cool control represents an effective pathway to enhance the thermodynamic and operational performance of liquid CO 2 energy storage systems.

title: Unveiling electric vehicle charging demand patterns in medium-sized urban areas through detailed and comprehensive statistical analysis of empirical data to support efficient infrastructure planning
Evaluation of electric cable-heated pavement using a thermo-mechanical numerical simulation model with different thermal management strategies
abstract: In recent decades, the integration of energy systems into civil engineering structures has gained growing importance. Among them, electric cable-heated pavements have been implemented to melt snow and ice on pavement surfaces. To improve their thermal efficiency, several thermal management strategies have been proposed. However, the coupled thermo-mechanical trade-offs induced by different thermal management strategies in electric cable-heated pavements, especially the time-dependent stress/strain concentrations around heating cables, remain quantitatively unclear. This study: (i) develops a three-dimensional transient thermo-mechanical numerical model for a standard electric cable-heated pavement; (ii) compares three representative thermal strategies (high thermal conductivity concrete surface layer, foam-concrete insulation layer, and asymmetric thermal insulation painting); and (iii) proposes a normalized multi-metric evaluation to balance thermal efficiency against mechanical cost. For the standard electric cable-heated pavement, the maximum von Mises stress reached 6 . 52 MPa . Based on this model, three thermal management strategies were compared, revealing clear trade-offs between thermal performance and thermo-mechanical responses. Foam-concrete insulation layer and asymmetric thermal insulation painting improved heat delivery towards the surface but intensified localized stress and strain concentrations around the cables. For example, foam-concrete insulation layer achieved the highest surface midpoint temperature, exceeding the baseline by 7 . 37 ° C , while increasing the maximum first principal stress σ 1 by 2.45 times (from 2.0 to 4 . 9 MPa ) near the cables. By contrast, high thermal conductivity concrete strategy slightly reduced the surface temperature while mitigating stress concentration, as evidenced by a reduction in the peak compressive principal stress magnitude from | σ 3 | = 14 . 1 to 10 . 2 MPa ( − 28 % ). A normalized multi-metric evaluation was then employed to balance thermal efficiency and mechanical cost, suggesting that asymmetric thermal insulation coating strategy offers a favourable overall compromise.

Optimal real-time management of aggregated EVs and batteries for technical support of residential virtual power plants using a binary TSO algorithm
abstract: To reduce carbon emissions by domestic customers, especially in transport needs, the UK government offers incentives to them for using zero-emission vehicles such as electric vehicles (EVs). Moreover, it encourages them to install rooftop photovoltaics and batteries. However, the increasing number of domestic EV chargers involves a significant investment in distribution network reconfiguration. Therefore, to support voltage regulation at distribution nodes, this paper offers optimal real-time management of aggregated large-scale smart chargers of EVs and batteries using a residential virtual power plant (VPP). In addition, the VPP maximizes the number of serving chargers and ensures fair charging for all connected EVs. Firstly, this paper proposes a novel binary transient search optimization (BTSO) algorithm for finding the optimal high-dimensional binary variable (switching EV chargers ON or OFF). Secondly, this paper presents a modified IEEE 33-bus system that includes around 1000 houses, each with an EV, a rooftop photovoltaic system, a static battery system, and household appliances. After that, the proposed BTSO-VPP is applied to monitor the buses’ voltages in the modified IEEE 33-bus system and coordinate the charging demand of all connected EVs. The simulation results revealed that the BTSO-VPP maintained the buses’ voltages above 94% compared to seven algorithms. Furthermore, BTSO-VPP guaranteed fair charging to all EVs, with charging priority given to EVs with low energy.

title: Experimental investigation of low-temperature desorption characteristics and control strategy of a low-pressure CO2 adsorption storage device for an adsorption-based compressed CO2 energy storage system

Dynamic simulation of offshore wind-to-green hydrogen power with thermochemical hydrogen co-production and underground storage in Ireland
abstract: Ireland’s National Hydrogen Strategy targets 2 GW of offshore wind capacity dedicated to hydrogen production by 2030. This study presents a dynamic 20-year simulation of an integrated wind-to-hydrogen-to-power system in which green hydrogen produced via proton exchange membrane electrolysis is stored in the depleted Southwest Kinsale gas reservoir and reconverted through a hydrogen-fuelled gas turbine to meet peak electricity demand. Four scenarios representing 10–25% of the planned offshore wind capacity are evaluated. A novel feature of the system is the integration of a vanadium–chlorine thermochemical cycle using gas turbine exhaust heat to co-produce additional hydrogen. The base-case system achieves an overall efficiency of 31.67%, increasing to 61.13% under advanced material assumptions. Net present values (NPV) remain negative under current assumptions (–€0.295 bn to –€1.051 bn), while levelised costs of energy (LCoE) range from €495 to €528 MWh⁻ 1 , indicating that the system is not economically viable as a private investment under current assumptions, primarily due to high capital costs and limited gas turbine utilisation. However, under improved material performance, the system achieves a positive NPV of €407 million and an LCoE of €259 MWh⁻ 1 . The results demonstrate that large-scale geological hydrogen storage combined with thermochemical hydrogen recovery is technically feasible for balancing offshore wind and enhancing energy security. While private-sector viability remains challenging under present conditions, future technology improvements could enable commercially viable large-scale renewable hydrogen power systems.

title: Improved syngas quality with biochar at mild conditions in a two-stage gasifier
abstract: Demand for syngas produced by gasifiers is increasing but its required quality varies depending on its use. Several technologies and operating conditions are therefore employed. For this reason, a two-stage gasifier was employed in this study to understand the influence of biochar at mild operating conditions for improving the syngas quality. This is of high relevance in several gasification and combustion applications, where the syngas goes through an increasing hot char bed and where reactions occur even in mild conditions. Wood pellets were gasified in a primary reactor at 725 °C with a steam to fuel ratio of 1.11. Wood, shrubland and rice husk chars were introduced in a secondary reactor as catalytic beds for syngas enhancement, with temperatures equal or lower than 800 °C and gas residence times in the secondary char bed of 0.27–0.54 s. Wood char produced the most H 2 , reduced tar content and CO concentration by improved water–gas shift, tar reforming and char gasification reactions. Rice husk reduced tar but barely affected the non-condensable gas composition and underwent almost no char gasification. Shrubland produced H 2 and reduced CO concentration as wood, but the tar reduction was lower. Increasing temperature and bed height improved water–gas shift, tar reforming and char gasification. The trifecta wood char, high temperature and bed height resulted in the best conditions for improving gas quality, obtaining up to a 35 % increase in H 2 /CO and 69 % tar reduction compared to the no catalytic bed reference case, which is especially relevant for specific applications and indicates positive catalytic biochar performance even at these mild conditions.

H2 separation from a reformed mixture by a hollow fibre membrane-based process: Experimental performance, predictive simulations, and cost analysis
abstract: H 2 separation and recovery play a key role in the industrial field due to the variety of pure H 2 applications and its relevance as clean fuel, energy carrier and feed material for many processes (e.g., fuel cells, ammonia and methanol production, oil refining etc.). Conventional gas separation methods include PSA, liquid absorption and cryogenic; however, membrane technology is proving to be a valid alternative that is increasingly developing in these last years. In this work, hollow fibre polymer membranes were used to concentrate H 2 from a syngas mixture, while also ensuring high recovery levels. Experiments, which were carried out considering pure gases (i.e., H 2 , CO 2 , CO and CH 4 ) and mixtures, reveal high H 2 /CO and H 2 /CH 4 ideal selectivity (e.g., 145 and 222, respectively), whereas a moderate H 2 /CO 2 value of about 4 was measured. In binary mixtures, H 2 permeation was improved by CO 2 and slowed down by the other species, showing a s behaviour similar to that of CO 2. Therefore, H 2 /gas selectivity resulted lower than the ideal value. A quaternary gas mixture representing a syngas stream was then analysed, achieving a maximum H 2 concentration of 93% paired with a recovery of 92%, when membrane process operates in two stages. A three-stage membrane system for H 2 and CO concentration from syngas was simulated, being able to achieve a H 2 purity of about 90% with a recovery higher than 98%. This process also allowed for a CO concentration from 13 up to about 71% in the final retentate product, where it was assumed that all CH 4 is recovered, since it was not experimentally detected in the permeate stream. An economic analysis showed that raw material was the main cost (68 – 74%), followed by compression (24 – 30%), whereas membrane cost was negligible (just 2% of the total).

title: Dispatch optimization and sizing of molten-salt power-to-heat systems in balancing electricity markets for industrial heat electrification
abstract: Decarbonization of industry remains a major barrier in the energy transition, with industrial process heat being a hard-to-abate source of emissions due to reliance on fossil fuels. To address this challenge, electrification of heat via power-to-heat technologies offers a promising pathway. This work investigates a power-to-heat system integrated with molten-salt thermal energy storage for medium-temperature industrial steam generation. A techno-economic assessment is conducted using a mixed-integer linear programming algorithm to optimize system dispatch under dynamic electricity pricing, including both day-ahead and balancing services markets. Multiple system configurations are evaluated to identify optimal sizing based on the levelized cost of heat, and results are benchmarked against conventional steam generation technologies. Results show that participation in balancing markets improves economic performance, significantly reducing the levelized cost of heat compared to day-ahead market operation alone. When ancillary services are included, the proposed system achieves operational cost savings between 0.9–4 M€/y against electric boiler. Despite growing interest in power-to-heat systems with thermal energy storage, existing studies on industrial steam applications remain scarce and typically do not consider multi-market participation. This study addresses this gap by developing an integrated framework for molten-salt-based power-to-heat systems supplying industrial steam, enabling coordinated dispatch in day-ahead and ancillary service markets under realistic electricity cost structures, including network tariffs. The results provide a basis for further research and future industrial deployment of flexible electrification solutions.

title: Flexible operation strategies for heat pumps in district heating systems using dynamic electricity prices
abstract: Electrifying the heating sector is essential for achieving global climate targets like the Paris Agreement’s 1.5 °C goal. In Germany, where 80 % of household energy goes to space heating and hot water, shifting to low-carbon solutions is crucial. Fossil-fuelled district heating networks can incorporate renewable energy via heat pumps, improving efficiency. Although heat pump design typically favours minimal temperature lifts, higher lifts can be economically viable with low electricity prices and abundant renewables. Adding thermal energy storage boosts operational flexibility. This study explores a flexible heat pump operation incorporating part load behaviour with a thermal energy storage in a German city’s district heating system to minimise costs and carbon dioxide emissions. Using a mixed-integer linear programming model, it examines the impact of temperature adjustments and storage on system efficiency. The results show that the integration of a heat pump in a district heating system reduces operating costs. Compared to a supply without a heat pump, with levelised cost of heating of 9.98 cent/kWh th and a fixed operating mode with costs between 9.96 cent/kWh th and 11.49 cent/kWh th , the flexible use results in lowest costs of 9.85 cent/kWh th , while also reducing overall CO 2 emissions. Using a full factorial sensitivity analysis, the levelised cost of heating ranged between 9.15 cent/kWh th in the best case and 10.37 cent/kWh th in the worst case for the selected configuration.

title: Dynamic simulation and operational feasibility of a solar-assisted thermal–mechanical vapor compression cycle with auxiliary subcooling for building cooling in hot desert climates

Waste heat driven direct contact membrane desalination coupled with reverse Brayton cycle: Techno-economic analysis and multi-objective optimization
abstract: This research examines the integration of a reverse Brayton cycle (RBC) used in a hydrogen liquefaction plant with a direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) system for waste heat recovery and freshwater production. Waste heat from RBC compressors is used to run the DCMD plant, with parametric analysis evaluating the effect of feed Reynolds number, permeate mass flow rate, module length and pinch temperature of heat exchangers on thermal and economic performance of the hybrid system. Both parallel and series multi-stage DCMD configurations are compared with higher feed and permeate flow rates enhancing the temperature polarisation coefficient and permeate flux. A maximum gained output ratio of 0.56 and a minimum specific thermal energy consumption of 1070 kWh/m 3 were achieved at a feed Reynolds number of 3050, with a permeate flow rate of 5 LPM. Economic analysis show that the capital cost of the DCMD plant accounts for 25% of the total capital cost, while waste heat recovery components account for 75% of the total capital cost. Almost 40% of the capital cost was used for permeate cooling, where in addition, lower permeate and higher feed flow rates reduced the levelized cost of water (LCOW). Further, LCOW and daily water production were chosen as optimization objectives in a genetic algorithm for multi-objective optimization, with optimal values calculated at 1.75 $/m 3 and 29.8 m 3 /day.

Optical and thermal performance analysis of ceramic foam solar receivers in parabolic dish solar collector assemblies: The role of collector geometrical and optical parameters and absorber and coating materials
abstract: Volumetric solar receivers perform a critical role in high-efficiency concentrated solar power systems, where effective absorption and conversion of concentrated solar radiation directly determine overall performance. This study presents a fully coupled pore-scale modeling framework that integrates Monte Carlo ray tracing with direct hydrothermal simulations on silicon carbide ( SiC ) and alumina ( Al 2 O 3 ) ceramic foam geometry acquired by computed tomography scans. The approach accurately captures radiative propagation, absorption distribution throughout the porous structure and subsequent fluid flow and heat transfer processes — all without resorting to empirical closure relations. A detailed parametric analysis examines the influence of parabolic dish concentrator parameters — rim angle, focal length, aperture radius, axial misalignment error and surface slope error — on the spatial distribution of solar flux and angle of incidence at a target probe surface (receiver entrance section). Results show that higher rim angles produce more intense but compact focal spots with wider angular dispersion, while even small misalignments ( δ f / f ≈ 0 . 006 –0.008) or surface slope errors rapidly degrade uniformity, increase optical spillage and promote non-uniform heating. Pore-scale simulations further reveal the impact of these radiation field variations and absorber material choice on receiver performance. Compared to silicon carbide, alumina foams exhibit lower optical efficiency due to poorer absorptivity but superior conversion of absorbed power to useful heat owing to reduced thermal conductivity limiting front-surface losses. Pyromark-coated alumina foam combines high absorptivity with low conductivity, yielding the highest optical and thermal efficiencies, elevated outlet temperatures and enhanced volumetric effect. Findings confirm that stronger volumetric heating does not necessarily improve thermal efficiency and highlight key design trade-offs for optimizing volumetric receivers.

title: Performance analysis and optimization of a novel integrated system combining the supercritical CO2 recompression cycle power plant and Carnot battery
An experimental study on the coupling effect of swirl ratio and injection timing in reactivity-controlled compression ignition gas engines
abstract: This study investigates the coupled effects of swirl ratio and start of injection on diesel–natural gas reactivity-controlled compression ignition, with particular focus on their unexplored interactions and their effects on combustion characteristics and emissions. Experiments were conducted on a single-cylinder research engine at a representative operating point, using four distinct intake port configurations to generate swirl. Diesel injection timing was swept between 34 and 47 crank angle degrees before top dead centre, constrained by misfire limits. In-cylinder pressure-based thermodynamic analysis, along with flow simulations, enabled the interpretation of how in-cylinder turbulence influences combustion. The results for the first time reveal that swirl has a limited effect on cylinder-bowl-initiated ignition but plays a dominant role in combustion development as it progresses into the squish region. A high swirl advanced combustion phasing by 5.4 degrees and increased the peak heat release rate by 20%, but reduced combustion efficiency by up to four percentage points compared with low-swirl configurations. This was attributed to excessive homogenisation of the mixture and greater wall heat losses, which also increased unburnt hydrocarbon and carbon monoxide emissions. Nitrogen oxides emissions correlated strongly with combustion timing and temperature, while remaining largely insensitive to swirl. There was no direct trade-off between nitrogen oxides and particulate emissions, with particulate mass remaining ultra-low. However, more premixed conditions (early injection and large swirl) produced more fine particles, with particulate number emissions double the EU Stage V limit. The neutral-port-only configuration, combining the lowest swirl with the highest average turbulent kinetic energy, yielded optimal performance, with the highest thermal efficiency, nearly 44%, and the lowest combined carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon emissions. The results demonstrate that reactivity-controlled compression ignition performance is governed by a balance between swirl- and tumble-driven flow structures rather than by swirl intensity alone, and that flow-injection optimisation can enable compliance with stringent off-road emission limits without exhaust aftertreatment.

title: Design of decarbonized energy systems for manufacturing sector considering Power-to-Liquid and gas
abstract: At the final stage of decarbonization society, synthetic fuel utilization system leveraging hydrogen and CCUS in the manufacturing sector is essential. However, developing this system presents challenges in elucidating interactions within Power-to-X technologies at high temporal resolution. To address this, we demonstrate a synthetic fuel energy system model that integrates variable renewable energy sources with final product demand in hard-to-abate manufacturing sectors. This model captures the relationship between variable renewable energy and Power-to-X processes, accounting for fluctuations at hourly resolution using mixed-integer linear programming. Additionally, we apply the Anderson-Schulz-Flory distribution to the syncrude produced via Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, constructing a framework for fuel demand that incorporates chemical synthesis constraints. The model analysis focuses on interactions between storage facilities and dispatchable sources. The introduction of wind power generation decreases fluctuation adjustment facility costs by smoothing power output variability. Batteries manage short-term fluctuations, while hydrogen and carbon dioxide storage facilitate long-term adjustments.

title: Editorial Board
