Absorption energy storage: energetic potentials for different processes, boundary conditions and working pairs
abstract: Absorption thermal energy storage systems hold potential for enabling seasonal storage of solar energy, addressing the challenge of sustainable heating in cold climates. These systems utilize sorption processes to store energy in form of a concentration gradient, thereby minimizing long-term energy dissipation. This study investigates the theoretical energetic potentials of such systems, focusing on single- and double-lift processes with and without crystallization. Key system parameters, including source and sink temperatures, are varied to evaluate their impact on energy storage density (ESD). The analysis incorporates pT-Diagrams and phase diagrams for various working pairs, including NaOH-H2O, LiCl-H2O, CaCl2-H2O, and LiBr-H2O, to determine optimal operating conditions.The findings reveal that NaOH-H2O achieves the highest theoretical ESD across all configurations, with crystallization enhancing storage capacity but introducing design complexity. While double-lift systems show potential at high-temperature lifts between source and sink, single-lift processes remain more efficient at lower lifts. By presenting a comprehensive thermodynamic assessment, this work contributes to a deeper understanding of the role of closed absorption storage systems in the energy transition, offering insights for future research and development.

title: Physics-data driven surrogate model development and evaluation for multi-objective optimization of thermally activated building envelopes
Development and validation of a predictive SITurb combustion model for a heavy-duty turbocharged direct-injection hydrogen SI engine
Improvement of consecutive Melting/Solidification with reduced lengths of innovative fins for mobile thermal Batteries
abstract: Mobilized thermal energy storage (M-TES) systems are promising to support the decarbonization of residential heating and thermal conditioning to reduce energy consumption via incorporating the industrial waste heat. This study aims to improve both the charging and discharging performance of M-TES systems, which inherently involve consecutive melting and solidification processes. T-, Y-, and V-shaped fin configurations with various geometric ratios and placements are numerically investigated under identical conditions using ANSYS Fluent in a two-dimensional horizontal domain. The results show that increasing fin volume does not necessarily improve thermal performance unlike the results of conventionally used straight fin structures, as excessive fin length can suppress natural convection and reduce effective phase change material (PCM) utilization. Among all cases, toplocated Y-shaped configurations provide the best overall performance, reaching up to 34 % liquid fraction within 30 min of melting while also exhibiting superior solidification behavior. Moreover, contrary to common design assumptions, top-located fins can achieve comparable melting and solidification performance to bottom-located configurations, and even superior behavior when Y-shaped fins are employed. In addition, compared to optimized (4-fin) configurations from our previous work, the selected Y-shaped design reduces total solidification time by up to 63 % and 78 % when the tube wall temperature is set as 30 degrees C and 97.7 degrees C, respectively. Furthermore, a shorter fin configuration (Y)-Top-LT = 52 mm achieves comparable performance with 18.7 % less fin material, enabling higher PCM utilization, lower system weight, and reduced cost. These findings indicate that appropriately designed fin structures can simultaneously enhance thermal performance and technoeconomic feasibility, making them particularly suitable for medium-temperature thermal energy storage applications.

title: Experimental, characterization, and process parameters optimization using RSM of two-step pyro-gasification of native and Ni-Fe impregnated coconut husk with recycle stream
Is lateral heat conduction effect significant in thermal regulation and energy recovery using a TEG array? An analysis of power electronics cooling in flight vehicles
Electro-thermal-aging framework for immersion cooling battery modules with 3D to 1D model reduction and vehicle level integration
abstract: Efficient thermal management of electric vehicle battery modules requires modeling approaches that capture spatial thermal gradients while remaining computationally efficient for system level evaluation under realistic driving conditions. This study presents a multi-scale electro-thermal-aging framework based on systematic three-dimensional (3D) to one-dimensional (1D) model reduction for a 360 cell immersion-cooled lithium-ion battery module integrated into a complete electric vehicle model. Convective heat transfer coefficients and pressure losses extracted from CFD simulations are implemented in a reduced 24-node thermal model representing coolant flow direction effects. Heat generation is obtained from an experimentally validated electrochemical model, and a temperature-dependent degradation model capturing solid-electrolyte interphase growth, cathode film formation, and active material isolation is coupled to each node to enable spatially resolved aging prediction. The reduced model reproduces 3D temperature distributions within 2 °C while decreasing computational time. Vehicle level simulations under NEDC and US06 driving cycles demonstrate that immersion cooling maintains high thermal uniformity, resulting in less than 0.5 % state of health variation across module nodes. The proposed framework provides a computationally efficient tool for evaluating immersion cooling architectures and quantifying their impact on thermal performance, degradation, and vehicle range under realistic driving scenarios.

title: Solar-driven ejector cooling under transient operation and Hot-Climate Constraints: A critical review and operability-based framework
abstract: Solar-driven ejector refrigeration systems (SERS) use low- to medium-grade thermal energy to enable compressor-free cooling for sustainable cooling. In principle, SERS performance should be comparable to that of mechanical systems; however, real-world performance is affected by solar transience and ambient temperature, which often drive the ejector out of its critical (double-choked) operating regime, thereby severely limiting its widespread deployment. This review proposes a transition from the study of SERS performance on a steady-state, peak-performance basis to an operationally based analysis that accounts for time-dependent, transient, and climate-dependent operating conditions. Specifically, the relationship between the system-level variables (temperatures of the generator T g , condenser T c , and evaporator T e ) and the flow regime transitions through the ejector demonstrates the importance of backpressure critical limits in ensuring entrainment stability and the feasibility of cooling. The proposed unified operability framework is based on dynamic operational metrics, such as backpressure margin, and the critical regime residence time, thereby enabling valid comparisons across studies and climatic conditions. The coupling of solar variability, condenser temperature penalties, and system trajectories in the T g − T c − T e coordinate system indicates that climatic conditions are the primary limiting factor for operational feasibility. Mitigation strategies for off-design loads, such as thermal energy storage, adaptive ejector configurations, and system-level control, are examined for their ability to extend operational parameters rather than improve peak efficiency. Finally, the working fluids used in SERS are also reviewed in this framework to emphasize that their suitability depends on how well they operate within the ejector operating limits and their robustness to fluctuations in condenser temperature. This review therefore establishes a unified operability framework linking thermodynamics, ejector flow regimes, and climatic constraints. The primary SERS challenge is not maximizing peak efficiency, but rather providing stable operation under real-world, time-varying, ambient conditions. The proposed operability-based framework provides a single basis for climate-responsive design, performance comparison, and system optimization. Because of this, the transition of SERS from laboratory-scale study into practical, reliable, real-world cooling applications will be easier to achieve.

title: Predictive maintenance of large-scale building cooling plants under operational constraints: A review
Anode water management and parameter control in an ejector-based proton exchange membrane fuel cell system
An analytical reliability model for PV systems
abstract: This paper proposes an analytical reliability assessment framework for photovoltaic (PV) systems that overcomes several limitations of existing reliability modeling approaches. The developed method captures the reliability characteristics of multiple PV system components and their interactions under realistic operating conditions. Failures at the substring and bypass diode levels are explicitly modeled. The operation and availability of the maximum power point tracking (MPPT) unit are also incorporated, particularly addressing the challenges arising from its interaction with bypass diode function. In addition, the model considers wear-out failures of critical power electronic components, including the inverter and MPPT unit, whose degradation is estimated using physics-of-failure principles. The proposed framework derives key PV reliability indices and is validated against Monte Carlo simulations for Copenhagen and Phoenix, showing excellent agreement with minimal error ( < 0.012%) and a 764×reduction in computation time. The proposed framework can assist in maintenance planning, component replacement scheduling, and the development of strategies to improve the long-term reliability and energy yield of PV power plants.

Techno-economic assessment of ammonia as a marine fuel: Incorporating dual-fuel operation and regulatory compliance costs
Electricity-hydrogen coordinated dispatch of pressurized oxy-fuel combustion systems: A bilevel Stackelberg approach with process-informed surrogates
Integration of green and turquoise hydrogen for blast furnace injection and power-to-X fuel production under EU renewable fuel regulation
abstract: Hard–to–abate industrial sectors such as fuel production and the iron and steel industry rely heavily on fossil carbon feedstocks and are major contributors to global greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions. Although hydrogen–based direct reduced iron routes offer deep long–term abatement for iron and steel, their high capital intensity creates a need for transitional options that enable earlier hydrogen deployment at lower risk. This study assesses direct hydrogen injection into existing blast furnaces (BF) and assesses whether combining renewable electrolytic (“green”) hydrogen with low–carbon methane–derived (“turquoise”) hydrogen within an integrated Hydrogen Valley can reduce system costs and renewable overcapacity while preserving substantial emission reductions. To assess this, a dynamic techno–economic Power–to–X optimisation model is applied to a 6,600 t hot metal day −1 BF steel mill integrated into a gigawatt–scale industrial Hydrogen Valley in Northern Finland, explicitly representing electricity markets, hydrogen production, storage and transport, and regulatory constraints for Renewable Fuels of Non–Biological Origin (RFNBO). Supplying a constant BF hydrogen demand of 7.65 tH 2 h −1 using only green hydrogen requires 380–430 MW of electrolyser capacity and 1,000–1,500 MW of wind power, resulting in hydrogen costs of €3.6–3.7 kgH 2 −1 , whereas integrating turquoise hydrogen improves system flexibility and reduces renewable overcapacity, and lowers hydrogen costs to €2.6–3.4 kgH 2 −1 ; however, future RFNBO quota requirements lower asset utilisation and increase costs to €2.9–3.7 kgH 2 −1 . Across all scenarios, GHG emissions decrease by approximately 20–21% per tonne of hot metal. Overall, hydrogen injection into existing BFs appears to be a cost–effective transitional pathway that supports early hydrogen infrastructure build–up while enabling meaningful near-term emission reductions and long–term progress toward fossil–free steel production.

title: Comparison of different biodiesel production technologies in the context of a soybean biorefinery
abstract: Biorefineries play an important role in the current energy scenario, serving as platforms for energy, biofuels, and high-value-added products generation, combining energy efficiency and sustainability. One of the most well-established biorefineries is the soybean biorefinery, where the oil can be used for fuel or food production. If used for fuel production, different technologies are available for biodiesel production, because much effort has been done in the last decades to overcome the limitations of the conventional route. Although no alternative technology has proven superior enough to justify a definitive market shift, some appear more promising than others and may benefit from certain economic contexts. However, a comparison between different technologies has never been made considering the whole biorefinery framework. Therefore, in this work, we evaluate how different biodiesel production technologies respond in the context of a soybean biorefinery. Homogeneous alkaline and acid catalysis, heterogeneneous chemical and enzymatic catalysis, and the supercritical process were compared for biodiesel production with methanol and ethanol. Literature process simulation references were used to supply the information needed for the mass balances solved, and hyphotetical scenarios created for those process alternatives for which data was not available. These hyphotecical scenarios must be considered preliminary estimates and would require further validation, but served to allow a broad comparison between the different process alternatives. Homogeneous alkaline transesterification with methanol is indeed the most economic alternative (NPV of US$ 54 million in the base case scenario) and it is clear that ethylic biodiesel is more expensive (∼1.5% on average) not only because of ethanol’s higher price, but also because of the higher utility costs required for its use. Into the whole soybean processing chain, although less profitable, the heterogeneous transesterification showed to be also economically feasible (NPV of US$ 26 to 29 million), while the acid homogeneous (US$ −124 to −117 million), enzymatic (US$ −92 to −89 million), and supercritical (US$ −48 to −49 million) transesterification routes are unfeasible. However, as demonstrated, the economic performance of any route is highly sensitive to input prices and product demands, and the least profitable technologies could become interesting in the future depending on the market constraints.

title: Economic and environmental benefits assessment of green ammonia co-firing at coal-fired power plants in large-scale wind and solar energy bases in Northwest China
Editorial Board
Aggregated electrolyzer modeling and coordinated frequency support of multi-GW offshore wind-hydrogen energy systems
abstract: Multi-gigawatt offshore wind-hydrogen energy systems (OWHESs) extend conventional high-voltage direct-current (HVDC)-connected offshore wind power plants (WPPs) by integrating large-scale electrolyzer plants (ELPs), offering a promising decarbonization path through coupling clean offshore wind and green hydrogen. For OWHES dynamic assessment, ELP models scalable to large plant capacities are needed to preserve key electrical dynamics and capture interactions with HVDC links and WPPs. However, existing studies lack an explicit scale-up modeling method for constructing such models, limiting integrated OWHES dynamic assessment. Moreover, existing frequency controls for HVDC-connected WPPs and ELPs are separately developed, without coordinating their complementary responses, leaving OWHES frequency support under-exploited. To address these gaps, this paper develops a module-based aggregated ELP modeling method and a coordinated fast frequency control strategy for OWHESs. The proposed model derives a capacity-scalable plant-level ELP equivalent through an explicit module-to-plant parameter-aggregation formulation, retaining stack, converter, hydrogen-buffer, and controller dynamics while reducing complexity. The proposed control coordinates HVDC, WPP, and ELP active-power responses, enabling fast frequency support and smooth, automatic post-support recovery. An integrated 2 GW OWHES model is established on a real-time simulator for system-level verification. Results demonstrate that the aggregated ELP model reproduces the detailed model with only 0.02% maximum power-response error, verifying the capacity-scalable ELP modeling. Compared with existing methods, the proposed frequency control achieves higher frequency nadir, lower frequency-change rate, and shorter settling time while avoiding deadband-induced oscillations. These results provide a modeling and control basis for offshore wind–hydrogen hubs to enable renewable power–hydrogen coupling while providing grid support.

title: Unveiling the techno-economic realities of renewable-integrated electrified hydrogen production: a comparative analysis of electrified steam methane reforming and solid oxide electrolysis
How pressure control shapes heat transfer and economic viability: A time-varying assessment of a zeotropic Kalina cycle system 11 under fluctuating waste heat
Dynamic thermodynamic modeling and performance analysis of solar adsorption ice production systems using a TRNSYS-based approach
Water leaching and microwave-induced torrefaction of tropical agricultural residues: Ash reduction, fuel quality enhancement, and integrated sustainability assessment
Pressure-regulated pool boiling for lithium-ion batteries based on a thermo-lifetime-economic coupling framework
abstract: Pool boiling cooling offers strong potential for lithium-ion battery thermal management due to its high-efficiency phase-change heat transfer. However, most existing studies are limited to atmospheric pressure, and the coupled effects of pressure on thermal behaviour, battery lifetime, and economic performance remain unclear. In this study, a thermo-lifetime-economic coupling model is developed and experimentally validated through pressure-controlled pool boiling cooling of a battery module over a pressure range of 20–100 kPa. The results show that pool boiling significantly outperforms natural air-cooling, reducing the maximum temperature from 88.8 °C to 45.6 °C (48.6%) and the temperature difference from 9.3 °C to 3.1 °C (66.7%) at 2.5C. Further pressure reduction enhances thermal performance by lowering the saturation temperature and promoting earlier nucleate boiling. When the pressure decreases from 100 kPa to 20 kPa, the maximum temperature and temperature difference are further reduced by 26.3% and 38.7%, respectively, leading to a lifetime improvement of up to 65.1%. However, this improvement is accompanied by a substantial increase in auxiliary power consumption, which rises by more than 14.6 times, resulting in a strong thermo-economic trade-off with diminishing returns at low pressures. Furthermore, system scale critically affects economic feasibility. Pressure reduction increases cost at small scales but becomes favourable beyond a critical scale due to the growing contribution of lifetime-related cost. These results show that pressure regulation can improve pool boiling battery cooling, but the operating pressure should balance thermal performance, lifetime, and energy consumption.

title: Exploring the flexibility potential of office building with air-to-water heat pumps in the Mediterranean climate
abstract: Buildings account for a significant share of energy consumption, making heat pumps and renewable energy key solutions for decarbonization. However, the variability of renewables poses challenges to grid stability and reliability. In this context, heat pumps, when coupled with other renewable systems, offer substantial potential for demand response programs by modulating their electricity consumption according to external signals such as energy prices and grid constraints. This study investigates the potential of demand response programs in a tertiary sector building. A dynamic simulation was conducted in TRNSYS, accurately modeling building envelopes with different insulation levels, the multi-stage heat pump, the photovoltaic-battery system and their integrated controls. The analysis evaluates both price-based and photovoltaic-driven demand response strategies by dynamically and statically varying the temperature setpoints of the thermal zones and the thermal energy storage. Four strategies are assessed against a reference scenario, and their impacts on electricity consumption and human comfort are evaluated. The most effective demand response approach is achieved by combining thermal energy storage setpoint adjustments with the enhanced insulation configuration and night-time ventilation, increasing annual acceptable thermal comfort to 81.22% and reducing annual electricity consumption by up to 28.22%. When coupled with a photovoltaic-battery system, the interaction between on-site solar generation and optimized thermal loads further enhances grid benefits, achieving a reduction in annual electricity drawn from the grid of up to 59.89%. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrated solutions for grid flexibility with limited comfort impacts.

Sizing and techno-economic assessment of an offshore wind-powered plant for e-methanol and e-dimethyl ether considering equipment flexibility
abstract: Offshore wind-to-X plants are promising routes to produce low-carbon e-fuels, but their design is constrained by renewable intermittency, equipment operability limits, and strict platform space and payload boundaries. Offshore wind-powered Power-to-X and carbon capture and utilisation (PtX/CCU) plants must be sized not only for nominal throughput, but also to remain operable under renewable intermittency and the physical constraints of offshore platforms. This work proposes a workflow for flexibility-constrained sizing and techno-economic assessment of an offshore PtX/CCU plant integrated on a repurposed North Sea platform (D18a). A design operating point is selected using the month-average wind-farm capacity factors and explicit operability limits. The plant is then sized at the resulting design point and stress-tested under the full seasonal capacity-factor profile with fixed equipment sizes. The workflow is demonstrated for two product cases: e-methanol and a comparative e-DME case. Offshore feasibility screening based on footprint and topside weight indicates that all cases fit within the nominal D18a constraints, with platform-level metrics dominated by balance-of-plant systems, particularly PEM electrolysis arrays (footprint) and short-duration storage (weight). A discounted cash-flow analysis yields levelised discounted costs of 2178~\$/t for the best e-methanol configuration and 3181~\$/t for the best e-DME configuration. Cost breakdown and one-at-a-time sensitivity results show that PEM CAPEX, project lifetime and electricity price are the primary DLCoP drivers, followed by the discount rate. Overall, the proposed workflow provides a practical and generalisable method to translate renewable variability and equipment flexibility limits into defensible offshore plant sizing decisions and consistent techno-economic comparisons across e-fuel options.

title: Experimental study on heat pump cycle-based cabin waste heat recovery for battery electric vehicles

Surrogate-assisted optimisation of a dual-source geothermal organic rankine cycle under CO2/NCG variability: optimal split-ratio and setpoints
abstract: Geothermal Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) plants are increasingly required to operate flexibly to support power systems with high penetrations of variable renewables. Off-design performance is strongly influenced by non-condensable gas (NCG) disturbances and operating constraints that introduce non-smooth response regions associated with phase-change limits and heat-transfer bottlenecks. This study develops a surrogate-assisted offline optimisation framework for a dual-source (flash-binary) geothermal ORC and quantifies how optimal setpoints shift under varying CO 2 /NCG disturbance intensity. A physics-consistent DWSIM (open-source process simulation) model generates a 5,000-point dataset spanning feasible operating regimes; a Random Forest surrogate achieves R 2 = 0.959, root mean square error (RMSE) = 283.4 kW and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) = 0.39%, capturing the non-smooth thermodynamic response surface. The surrogate is embedded in a Powell-Conjugate Hybrid Evolution Strategy (PCH-ES) combining Differential Evolution for global exploration with Powell refinement for local exploitation, producing a pre-computed disturbance-indexed setpoint scheduling table. Results identify an optimal split-ratio (SR*) band: in the low-CO 2 regime the optimum lies near SR* = 0.671; above approximately 1.8% CO 2 it shifts to SR* = 0.710, providing a disturbance-aware design rule for distributing working fluid between steam- and brine-side heat recovery. Net power declines 13% across the studied disturbance range (27,612 to 23,921 kW) as a thermal-capacity effect. The optimisation also identifies a thermodynamic knee in working-fluid circulation near 315 to 320 kg/s, beyond which additional pumping yields diminishing returns. The resulting offline setpoint lookup provides actionable scheduling guidance for disturbance-aware supervisory operation without requiring real-time modelling software.

title: System-level assessment of electrodialysis desalination as a flexible Power-to-Water load in isolated renewable islands
abstract: The large-scale integration of renewable energy sources in isolated power systems often results in significant electricity surpluses, while freshwater production remains highly energy-intensive and dependent on fossil fuels. This study proposes and assesses a Power-to-Water system that converts surplus photovoltaic electricity into potable water through electrodialysis desalination. The system is applied to Lampedusa Island, Italy, a remote Mediterranean island not connected to the mainland grid and currently supplied by diesel-based power generation and reverse osmosis desalination. The proposed layout integrates a 22 MW photovoltaic field, a 4.62 MW electrodialysis plant, 25 MWh lithium-ion battery storage, a freshwater storage basin, and a biodiesel production chain based on microalgae cultivation to further reduce fossil fuel consumption. A comprehensive dynamic model of the integrated energy–water system is developed in TRNSYS using high-resolution load profiles and component-level models. Simulation results show that the proposed configuration covers 99.35% of the island’s electricity demand through renewable electricity and supplies the entire freshwater demand through renewable-powered desalination. In particular, 97.46% of the freshwater demand is produced through the Power-to-Water strategy, while the remaining share is covered by the backup operation of the electrodialysis unit. Compared with the reference configuration, the proposed system achieves a primary energy saving of 92.62%, reduces operating costs by 34.09%, and reaches a simple payback period of 8.6 years. The levelized cost of electricity decreases to 0.160 €/kWh, while the levelized cost of water is 3.66 €/m 3 , slightly higher than the reference reverse-osmosis-based configuration. The results indicate that electrodialysis-based Power-to-Water systems can provide system-level value in isolated renewable islands by acting as flexible loads for surplus renewable electricity, although their practical deployment remains dependent on technology maturity, component costs, and site-specific constraints.

title: Negative carbon emissions of CO production via a CO2-coupled biomass chemical looping process
A cleaner energy system designed to cover energy and other needs for an Indigenous community
abstract: In this study, in order to address the issue of remote Indigenous communities in Canada, which have trouble accessing essentials, such as continuous energy and food supply, an integrated, off-grid, novel and sustainable energy system has been developed. This energy system, where hydrogen will serve as an energy storage medium, will be capable of providing, especially electricity, clean fuel, fresh water, and enabling some soilless agriculture operations and greenhouse heating. A cleaner solution is proposed by incorporating hydrogen and renewables into such locations, where they have an existing energy supply problem. After producing electricity from bifacial solar panels and wind turbines in accordance with Arctic Grade, the generated electricity will be delivered to an electrolyzer, where hydrogen will be produced, and the rest will be delivered to electrically driven processes. Hydrogen is utilized as sustainable transportation fuel and as an energy storage medium during periods of surplus renewable energy, and it is utilized to meet electricity demand when renewable generation is insufficient. Detailed energy and exergy analyses are performed; static and dynamic analysis results are presented and discussed comprehensively. Renewable energy system capacities are determined, and exergy destruction rates, entropy generation rates, and parametric analyses are performed. Moreover, different energy supply scenarios, including solar–wind hybrid, purely wind-based, and fully solar-based options, are evaluated. A cost assessment is performed for each scenario, and the associated emission reductions are compared with the current diesel-based supply. The study results reveal that the hybrid and purely wind-based systems achieve better performance than the fully solar-based option and offer economically and thermodynamically competitive alternatives for remote Indigenous communities. However, diesel replacement remains challenging because hydrogen storage costs strongly affect system feasibility. If lower-cost storage options, such as underground hydrogen storage, are available, these systems can become more effective candidates for replacing diesel-based electricity generation.

title: Medium- and long-term contract energy decision-making for hydro–wind–solar complementary systems under multivariate uncertainty

Origami-based and oscillator design of triboelectric nanogenerators in smart bridge expansion joints for self-powered infrastructure monitoring systems
abstract: This paper reports, for the first time, the integration of triboelectric energy nanogenerators (TEGs) into bridge expansion joints to harness traffic-induced mechanical vibrations for sensor self-powering. The smart expansion joint adopts non-resonating origami-based TEGs to generate power from the displacement induced by direct tyre contact (DC-NTEGs), and oscillator origami-based TEGs to harness the residual vibration transmitted outward from the contact regions (RV-OTEGs). A mathematical model was developed to incorporate the origami design into the V-Q-x theory. Benefiting from the compact design, a high power density of 2.81 W/m 3 can be obtained from a 10-fold DC-NTEGs under an excitation of 9 mm peak-peak displacement at 5 Hz. The stiffness of the origami structure is displacement dependent, rendering a Duffing nonlinear oscillator with origami structures as structural springs. The resonant frequency of RV-OTEGs increases with the increased spring precompression and excitation magnitude. With a 10 mm precompression on the 10-fold origami structures, the RV-OTEG produces a power density of 0.23 W/m 3 at the resonant frequency of 7.5 Hz. Following field-test verification of both energy harvesting performance and structural durability of a smart expansion joint prototype, the origami-based TEGs were numerically evaluated in a full-scale bridge expansion joint. 12 DC-NTEGs and 16 RV-OTEGs were deployed within the joint, excited by a simulated 10-min traffic. With rectification, the DC-NTEGs collectively produce an energy density of 0.60 µJ/g 2 , and a doubled energy density of 1.14 µJ/g 2 is obtained for RV-OTEGs.

title: Recovery strategy optimization for heterogeneous energy systems in coal chemical industrial parks based on resilience assessment
Fully coupled characteristics analysis of external combustion and oscillatory flow of Free-Piston Stirling engine
Restart without re-inoculation: Demonstrating biofilm resilience in a pilot-scale biological methanation system after 1.5 years of inactivity
abstract: Biological methanation of hydrogen (H 2 ) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) in trickle bed reactors (TBR) is considered a promising technology for energy conversion, especially in the context of energy storage via Power-to-Gas (PtG). This study investigates the restart of a pilot-scale thermophilic TBR after 1.5 years of uncontrolled dormancy under real wastewater treatment plant conditions to upgrade raw biogas from the local digester to synthetic natural gas quality (CH 4 > 95 %). Molecular biological investigations have indicated that it might be feasible to recommend the operation of the reactors, even following a highly protracted period of inactivity. The results demonstrate that the reactor can be successfully reactivated without re-inoculation, indicating a high resilience of the biofilm-based microbial community. Following the addition of digester supernatant as a nutrient and buffer source, methane concentrations above 95 % were achieved within a few hours. Stable operation was strongly linked to maintaining NH 4 + concentrations above 400 mg/L and controlled pH conditions, highlighting the importance of process stabilization during restart. Furthermore, the integration of a 5 kW AEM electrolyzer enabled on-site hydrogen production, demonstrating the feasibility of coupling biological methanation with renewable energy supply (e.g., through photovoltaic). Overall, the results provide new insights into rapid reactor restart, process resilience, and the practical implementation of PtG systems under real operating conditions.

title: Numerical and experimental study of integrating heat pipe cooling in semi-transparent photovoltaic windows
Performance analysis and optimization of a combined system based on recompression transcritical CO2 power cycle and transcritical ejector refrigeration cycle for waste heat recovery of gas turbine
Multi-objective thermodynamic optimization of fractal honeycomb cooling structures: A unified methodological framework
abstract: This study follows a comprehensive multi-objective methodology for optimizing cooling geometries by synthesizing hydraulic, thermal, and entropic performance metrics. The approach is validated through the analysis of honeycomb heat sinks derived from a fractal iteration equation. Three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted over a Reynolds number range of 10 to 5 x 10 4 to quantify the trade-offs between geometric complexity and thermodynamic utility. The proposed framework assesses designs via the integration of a synergy coupling number, exergy destruction number, thermodynamic impedance number, entropy augmentation number, and a defined peak thermal performance number. Results indicate that reliance on single-variable optimization may lead to misleading conclusions, often failing to capture system inefficiencies. On the other hand, the proposed methodology effectively recognizes the distinction between systems that are merely hydraulically permeable and those achieving a sustainable thermodynamic equilibrium. Ultimately, the framework identifies the specific geometric complexity and operational Reynolds number that represent the engineering optimum. At this operational locus, the system maximizes utility by equipartitioning frictional and thermal entropy generation while mitigating local thermal hotspots. This paradigm offers a robust tool for next-generation thermal management, redirecting design focus from simple heat flux maximization to the minimization of thermodynamic irreversibility.

title: Low-carbon combined heat and power system based on dual separation-enhanced solar methane reforming
Hydrogen-Gasoline E10 operation in the Series-Manufactured internal combustion engine at partial load
abstract: In response to increasingly stringent automotive CO 2 emission standards, researchers are exploring approaches to reduce CO 2 by blending carbon-free fuels with conventional gasoline. This study evaluates the effect of hydrogen addition on the performance and combustion thermodynamics of a series-production gasoline spark-ignition engine, focusing on heat-release rate, combustion phasing, and knock intensity, over a hydrogen share of 0 – 50 % by mass. Experiments were performed on a Nissan HR16DE passenger-car engine at a stoichiometric partial-load operating point (2500 rpm, IMEP 520–530 kPa), representing a stabilized mid-speed condition typical of everyday driving. The results show that increasing the hydrogen share requires retarding the spark timing to maximize indicated mean effective pressure. Brake thermal efficiency improved slightly, although a small decrease was observed at the highest hydrogen share. CO 2 emissions decreased proportionally to the hydrogen fraction in the fuel. Overall, hydrogen shortened the ignition delay, increased peak in-cylinder pressure, and no harmful knock was observed under the tested partial-load conditions. The distinguishing features of this work are the broad hydrogen range, independent hydrogen and gasoline dosing, and spark-timing optimization for each blend. The recommended hydrogen share is 20–59 % on an energy basis (10–33 % by mass). At optimal operation, the combustion center (CA) shifted to approximately 6 °CA ATDC, which can be used as a reference for spark-timing calibration. Accordingly, updating spark timing maps in the engine control software is recommended.

title: AI-assisted reliability-constrained design and operation optimization of biogas-to-methanol systems under feedstock uncertainty
An Otto-type electrochemical energy converter with decoupled heat and mass transfer for efficient low-grade heat utilization
Thermodynamic analysis of a coal-fired power plant integrated with Ca(OH)2/CaO thermochemical energy storage: Assessment of condensing and cogeneration modes
Revealing the risk–benefit mechanisms and applicability of multiple hybrid pumped-storage retrofit types under extreme meteorological scenarios
Peak-demand buffering via hydrogenation heat-to-power conversion in liquid organic hydrogen carrier systems
abstract: Renewable electricity is intermittent, motivating flexible buffering technologies. This study evaluates a thermally integrated system that recovers the exothermic heat of toluene hydrogenation in liquid organic hydrogen carrier (LOHC) systems and converts it into electricity for potential peak-demand buffering. Hydrogenation was carried out at 150–250 ℃ over Ru/Al 2 O 3 and Pt/Al 2 O 3 catalysts; Pt/Al 2 O 3 gave higher methylcyclohexane (MCH) selectivity and better thermal stability. A process model was built in Aspen Plus for a hydrogen processing capacity of 1,000 kg/h, and raising the steam pressure from 5 to 50 bar increased the net power output from 1,612 to 2,271 kW. A techno-economic analysis (TEA) using a stacked cost–revenue framework was applied to two configurations. In the co-production case (Case A), MCH is the primary product and the recovered heat yields electricity as a co-product, so the economics are set mainly by the MCH value. In the closed-loop case (Case B), electricity is the only product, giving a baseline levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of 0.51 $/kWh against an industrial benchmark of 0.09 $/kWh; lowering the dehydrogenation energy cost is the key lever toward grid parity. A life cycle assessment (LCA) gives 0.24–0.33 kg CO 2 -eq/kWh, below the grid average, provided that dehydrogenation energy use and material losses are controlled. LOHC facilities could therefore act not only as hydrogen-storage units but also as distributed power nodes that support grid flexibility.

Unlocking the grid flexibility potential of fifth-generation district heating and cooling systems through user-level demand-side strategies
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources is intensifying the need for energy flexibility solutions capable of supporting power grid stability. In this context, fifth-generation district heating and cooling (5GDHC) systems represent a promising yet still underexplored interface between urban thermal demand and electricity grids. This work investigates the potential of 5GDHC systems to provide energy flexibility services through demand-side management strategies implemented at building-user level. A physics-based dynamic modelling framework is developed, integrating building thermal demand calculation, heat pump performance modelling, and the representation of thermal energy storage and electrical batteries. Flexibility-oriented control strategies, including indoor temperature setpoint modulation, battery-assisted heat pump operation, and thermal energy storage integration, are simulated and assessed using dedicated flexibility indices for downward and upward load modulation and load shifting. The methodology is applied to a multi-user 5GDHC case study considering three alternative thermal balancing configurations: ground-coupled, groundwater-based, and solar-assisted solutions. The results of the simulative case study show that setpoint modulation enables short-term flexibility, achieving electricity load reductions of up to 37% and load increases of up to 26%. Battery integration enhances flexibility further, enabling load variations of 51–60%, while thermal energy storage achieves the highest performance, with load modulation exceeding 99% and load shifting fractions up to 54%. Flexibility provision is accompanied by primary energy savings of up to 11% and operating cost reductions of up to 14%, with groundwater-based configurations yielding the best overall performance. The proposed framework provides a robust tool to support the design and operation of flexible, low-carbon district energy systems.

title: Coupled optical-electrical-thermal performance analysis of CdTe photovoltaic glazing Façade under building shadow
A calibrated conditional GAN and hierarchical multi-task learning framework for combustion phasing prediction in spark-ignition engines
High-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage for low-carbon energy districts in Southern Europe
abstract: Seasonal thermal energy storage combined with district heating networks represents a promising pathway for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from urban heat supply. This study investigates the energy and environmental impacts of integrating a high-temperature aquifer thermal energy storage (HT-ATES) system into the district heating network of Tirano, northern Italy. The objective is to evaluate the contribution of HT-ATES to district heating decarbonization under hydrogeological conditions that are relatively unfavourable for thermal energy storage. The proposed system combines long-term thermal energy storage with renewable-based heat-supply technologies, including biomass boilers and a cogeneration plant, while retaining a diesel boiler solely as backup. System performance is simulated dynamically in TRNSYS 18 using real heating-demand data, whereas aquifer thermal behaviour is modelled in FeFlow to represent groundwater flow and heat transport. Despite the challenging storage conditions, the HT-ATES system achieves a thermal recovery efficiency of 25.2 % and enables the district heating network to operate with minimal reliance on fossil fuels. Under the assumption of climate-neutral renewable energy sources, the proposed configuration achieves carbon neutrality. These results demonstrate that meaningful decarbonization can be achieved even in non-ideal hydrogeological settings, highlighting the potential of HT-ATES to integrate surplus renewable thermal energy into district heating systems.

title: Thermo-economic assessment of a thermally balanced SOFC–SCBC–MED tri-generation system with dual-coupling waste heat recovery

Corrigendum to “Techno-economic assessment and comparison of Fischer–Tropsch and Methanol-to-Jet processes to produce sustainable aviation fuel via Power-to-Liquid” [Energy Conv. Manag. 315 (2024) 118728]
Optimal power allocation strategy for renewable hydrogen production considering usage-based stack degradation
abstract: This study investigates various power allocation strategies (PAS) for a multi-stack proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis plant (WEP) coupled with variable renewable energy (VRE, including solar photovoltaic (PV) and wind). A key contribution is the incorporation of a usage-based, current–density-driven degradation model, which more accurately captures the operational impacts of PAS on stack degradation and end-of-life replacement requirements compared to commonly used fixed annual degradation rates. The analysis also examines variations in the VRE-to-WEP capacity ratio, PV-to-wind mix, stack sizing, and overload. Results show that the optimal PAS depends strongly on these design parameters. In the base case without overload, the two-phase sequential-then-even PAS — which first brings stacks to their minimum operating level and then allocates power evenly — achieves the highest hydrogen (H 2 ) production and lowest specific energy consumption (SEC). Increasing the VRE:WEP ratio reduces the energy cost component of the levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH) initially, but beyond a threshold ratio the rising marginal cost of energy outweighs the gains. Allowing overload operation can improve H 2 production and reduce the LCOH under specific conditions, but accelerates stack degradation and raises replacement costs, often offsetting economic benefits. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering PAS, stack sizing, minimum operating levels, and VRE configuration when designing electrolyser systems for cost-effective green H 2 production.

title: Grey-box model of a short-term-operated pit thermal energy storage system
abstract: As the heat and power sectors become increasingly coupled, storing excess heat for later use is key to improvingenergy system efficiency. Pit thermal energy storage (PTES) systems, when integrated with district heating (DH)networks, offer a large storage capacity at a low investment cost. PTES systems can leverage stored heat for short-term operation to shave heat demand peaks. However, optimizing this dispatch requires accurate long-term forecastsof the available heat, which depend on reliable models of the pit’s thermal dynamics.To this end, we develop a grey-box model based on the heat transfer equation in fluids. By spatially discretizingthis equation, we describe the time evolution of water temperature at different depths within the pit. A stochasticnoise term is added to account for model uncertainties. This approach combines physically consistent dynamics withstatistical parameter estimation. On real-world operational data, the model achieves a root mean squared error of0.1◦C for one-hour ahead and 1.5◦C for one-week ahead forecasts. This performance stems from careful attention tonumerical stability of parameter estimation tools. Implicit differential equation solvers ensure robust state propagationover long time horizons, while automatic differentiation provides accurate gradients for optimization. The resultinghigh-fidelity model is well-suited for integration into economic dispatch tools, supporting more efficient DH operation.

title: Technoeconomic analysis of steel production with electric thermal energy storage
abstract: The iron and steel industry is an important manufacturing sector and one of the largest energy consumers in the United States and globally. Hydrogen direct reduction of iron ore (H2DRI) is considered a promising process that could enhance domestic steel production. This process requires hydrogen inlet temperatures up to 950 °C to drive the endothermic reduction of the iron ore pellets. In this work we investigate the technoeconomic performance of an H2DRI plant using electric thermal energy storage (ETES) technologies for the hydrogen heating, compared to conventional natural gas fired heaters, hydrogen fired heaters, and electric hydrogen heaters. A technoeconomic analysis framework for the plant is developed and used in multiple case studies, covering different hydrogen prices, grid electricity profiles, and financing scenarios. The levelized cost of steel production is found out to be in the range of $775–950/mt, which is mostly inside the benchmarked steel price of $941/mt. ETES-based hydrogen heating is found to be in par with conventional natural gas fired heaters, and cheaper than hydrogen fired heaters and electric hydrogen heaters. The major cost drivers are the iron ore and hydrogen feedstock, followed by the hydrogen compression and heating capital. Several insights and suggested future directions are identified.

title: Novel experimentally validated prediction models for canal-site photovoltaic performance enhancement using active water cooling techniques in semi-arid climate
Experimental investigation on self-starting mechanism and power characteristics of Darrieus-Savonius vertical-axis hydrokinetic turbines under ultra-low flow velocities
Pore scale thermal response and transient energy evolution in a porous wick evaporator during pre-dryout

Experimental investigation and intelligent optimization of an integrated low-temperature economizer–air preheater–steam-electric dual-drive waste-heat recovery system in a 1000 MW coal-fired unit

Process analysis of sustainable methanol production using super-dry reforming: techno-economic, life-cycle, and exergy analysis
Renewable energy integration and modeling approaches in district heating networks: a review
abstract: Integrating renewable energy sources (RES) into district heating networks (DHNs) is a promising strategy for achieving global decarbonization goals. This requires an understanding of viable RES options for DHNs to guide context-specific selection. Additionally, investors and operators must assess the performance of RES-based DHNs, necessitating accurate models to support optimal investment decisions and operational strategies. This paper addresses both of these aspects. We present a review of the integration of five selected RES into DHNs, alongside various modeling techniques used to analyze and characterize them. A multi-label classification of modeling approaches is proposed based on a detailed literature review and technological insights. A decision tree is included to help select an appropriate modeling technique based on specific objectives/tasks in DHNs. Furthermore, we discuss the integration pathways for RES in DHNs. Also, a qualitative overview of RES in DHNs is presented across six key criteria: cost, efficiency, storage potential, system complexity, flexibility, and carbon footprint. A multi-criteria overview suggests that hybrid systems seem to offer a more practical and effective solution for integrating RES into DHNs. However, their technical, economic, and environmental performance remains highly context dependent.

title: Experimental and multi-objective optimization of a hybrid battery thermal management system integrating dual-layer graded composite phase change materials with wavy liquid cooling plate
Biomethanol production from landfill biogas: A techno-economic comparison of different potential pathways with real landfill biogas feed data for a production plant in South-Spain
abstract: The production of biomethanol from landfill biogas represents a promising pathway for renewable applications, yet its economic feasibility remains a critical challenge. Herein we present a novel study aimed at conducting a techno-economic analysis to obtain biomethanol out of a landfill biogas produced in South-Spain. Four production pathways are evaluated: (i) dry reforming as a baseline case; (ii) a syngas upgrading route via reverse water–gas shift; (iii) green hydrogen feed to yield more biomethanol; and (iv) tri-reforming based on steam produced within the process and oxygen from the biogas itself. By this, a more realistic approach to a higher value-added utilization of landfill biogas is demonstrated to be viable. Process simulations were conducted in Aspen Plus, and economic performance was assessed in Excel through Net Present Value (NPV) and Minimum Selling Price (MSP) as key indicators. Results prove that tri-reforming technology significantly increases biomethanol production while slightly increasing material costs, thus achieving a competitive MSP value of 0.86€/kg with a positive NPV compared to green hydrogen (MSP = 0.95€/kg), reverse water–gas shift (MSP = 1.16€/kg) and dry reforming (MSP = 1.39€/kg). Sensitivity analysis highlights the influence of reforming heating and labour expenses on economic performance. This study sheds light on the existing literature missing case studies based on real feed biogas conditions, a gap that needs to be addressed since the future sustain of producing biomethanol will largely depend on accurate assessments to process biogas.

title: Fatty acid-specific lipotoxicity limits microalgal lipid productivity through photosynthetic membrane stress: An insight from microalgal proteome responses
Multidimensional climate benchmarks reshape resilience assessment for pumped hydro storage-supported hybrid energy systems under climate extremes
Thermodynamic assessment of a novel liquid direct air capture system integrated with natural gas reforming for synergistic methanol production
Risk-aware energy management of variable-frequency marine HVAC systems under modal spectral constraints
Carbon negative syngas production with controlled H2/CO ratio from fruit processing byproducts via CO2-assisted pyrolysis
Modeling the optimal technological mix for buildings’ energy demand: A multi-period approach under decarbonization pathways
abstract: Decarbonizing the building sector requires integrated approaches capable of capturing interactions between technologies, energy carriers, and spatial heterogeneity. This study develops a multi-period cost-optimization framework to identify the optimal technological mix for space heating, cooling, and domestic hot water under long-term decarbonization pathways. The model combines high-resolution spatial demand assessment with a national-scale optimization implemented in the open-source Oemof framework, explicitly representing retrofit measures, hybrid systems, and renewable-based technologies. The framework is applied to the Italian building sector over 2021–2050 under emission constraints. Results show a progressive phaseout of gas boilers in favor of electric and hybrid heat pumps, district heating, and biomass systems, with strong regional differentiation driven by climatic conditions. Building retrofit plays a central role, enabling around 30% energy savings and facilitating the deployment of low-temperature technologies. The transition entails an additional cumulative system cost of approximately €320 billion (€12100 per household), driven by higher capital investments and partially offset by reduced operating costs. The proposed approach provides a transparent and flexible tool to support the design of cost-effective and spatially tailored decarbonization strategies.

title: Performance evaluation and operational optimization of multi-form calcium-based materials for solar thermochemical energy storage
Prospective life cycle assessment of methanol synthesis from plasma-assisted waste gasification with carbon capture
abstract: The decarbonisation of chemical production requires moving away from fossil feedstocks towards alternatives. Methanol, a versatile C1 compound and potential alternative fuel or chemical feedstock, is traditionally synthesised from fossil resources like natural gas. Alternatively, it can be produced from biomass but also in circular waste-valorisation systems. Despite growing technical interest, comprehensive environmental sustainability evaluations are rare. This study presents a prospective life cycle assessment of methanol synthesis from plasma-assisted refuse-derived-fuel (RDF) gasification with integrated CO2 capture from waste-to-energy flue gas. Three process configurations are compared against natural gas reforming and biomass gasification reference pathways across 16 Environmental Footprint 3.1 impact categories. Background inventories were transformed using the Premise tool linked to the REMIND integrated assessment model under various future pathways from 2025 to 2050. Under current average European energy conditions, RDF gasification scenarios yield lower net climate change impacts than the natural gas reforming baseline, approximately 1.62–1.69 kg CO2 eq. per kg methanol. Electricity consumption, hydrogen supply, and end-of-life carbon release are the dominant contributors. Carbon capture benefits progressively offset energy-related burdens from around 2030 onwards, with net climate change impacts potentially falling as low as 0.58 kg CO2 eq. per kg methanol under ambitious decarbonisation pathways. At the same time, burden shifting from fossil energy use towards material resource consumption is projected as renewable energy technologies expand. Although its environmental performance strongly depends on the pace of energy system decarbonisation, plasma-assisted RDF gasification represents an environmentally viable route for fossil-free methanol production, complementing existing waste-to-energy infrastructure.

title: Internal flow evolution and energy dissipation in a high-speed cooling pump during rapid acceleration and deceleration processes
Techno-economic design and multi-objective optimization of an ammonia-fueled hybrid commercial vehicle with waste heat-driven onboard hydrogen production
Experimental investigation of titanium-based cold plates for thermoelectric generation (TEG) systems in sea environment
Hybrid energy sharing strategy of ultracapacitor assisted lithium-ion battery for electric vehicle
