The Biomass-to-Liquid (BtL) process via biomass gasification and Fischer-Tropsch synthesis is a technologically advanced route. We developed a framework to identify regionally favourable BtL process designs under environmental and economic constraints based on detailed process simulation. The process design choices include three configurations, four steam cycle options and two biomass feedstock types (bark or straw). The approach is applied to 82 NUTS2 regions across six Central European countries, accounting for spatial differences in, e.g., biomass availability, transport distance, and electricity price/emissions. Steam cycle mode and biomass type were identified as the most important variables for environmental impacts, whereas maximum plant size and configuration are crucial for cost. Two out of twelve process designs are suitable for balancing low climate change (CC) impact and cost, with the preferred choice depending on country-specific grid electricity and biomass type. By shifting from the economically preferred process design to the CC preferred design, the CC impact can be reduced by 5.0–83.5 % with cost increases of 1.0–17.5 %, depending on the region. The aforementioned adaptation generally coincides well with minimising burdens in other impact categories. Moreover, with a projected increase of renewables in the EU’s energy system by 2050, the preferred process design remains the same. Incorporating life cycle assessment alongside technical and economic objectives in the process design phase is therefore a long-term preferable approach for achieving climate neutrality by 2050.

title: Analysis of a flexible steam-generating heat pump with selected control strategies and integrated heat storage by steam accumulator
abstract: To unlock emissions reduction alongside demand-side flexibility in industry, steam-generating heat pumps must ensure a continuous and steady steam supply to users during power modulation events. This study aims to understand and characterise the steam supply dynamics and off-design performance of various heat pump control strategies that could be used to enact demand-side flexibility. Dynamic simulations of a 5 MW th steam-generating heat pump reveal a significantly different power modulation range, system efficiency impact and delivered steam fluctuations of the tested control strategies. Coupling a downstream steam accumulator is shown to enable demand‑response without compromising the continuity of steam. New accumulator design charts and sizing correction factors are derived to ensure this is the case, which traditional steady‑state analyses fail to do. Through a combination of control strategies, an overall 48 to 164 % power modulation range could be spanned by the heat pump. Variable rotational speed control enables turndown to 48 % power absorption and up to 11 % higher COP compared to rated conditions, and variable inlet guide vanes yield up to 164 % power absorption with COP reductions below 13 % from rated values. Development of compressor technology with improved surge and choke characteristics, as well as co-design of steam-generating heat pumps and thermal storage, are follow-up research directions towards promoting flexibility from the integrated system considered.

title: Investigating the aerodynamic fluctuations and wake characteristics of large floating vertical axis wind turbines under pitching motions
A centrifugal-switch mechanical-modulated power management interface for enhanced rotational energy harvesting under pulsed excitation
abstract: Within a single pulsed excitation event, rotational energy harvesters typically produce a decaying output, a substantial portion of which dissipates due to insufficient voltage magnitude to surpass the relatively high threshold of the conventional interface. To address this issue, a novel mechanical-modulated power management interface (MM-PMI) prototype without requiring external power was proposed in this work. The proposed MM-PMI prototype incorporates a mechanical switching system manipulated by centrifugal force and a low-loss electrical switching system to enable autonomous power-path reconfiguration at specific timing within the energy harvesting circuit containing two different energy storage modules. The proposed MM-PMI prototype operates independently of specific generation mechanisms, ensuring strong universality. A mathematical model of the proposed interface is established and validated, and its performances are evaluated and analyzed under diverse parametric conditions. Experimental results indicate that the switching systems can effectively enable the charge/discharge of electrical energy in the two storage modules at preset rotor speeds and voltage thresholds respectively. At a peak rotational speed of 400 rpm, the energy harvested by the load with the proposed interface can exhibit 10.82% and 51.39% improvement over the conventional full-bridge interface and Delon doubler interface in experiments, respectively. Under specific conditions, these improvements can be extended to 40.29% and 85.37%, respectively. In the application demonstration, the proposed interface enabled a multi-function timer to achieve an effective duration of 426.3 s under pulsed excitation provided by a pedestrian. These results therefore confirm the effectiveness of the proposed MM-PMI in enhancing energy conversion efficiency and highlight its strong market potential and scalability.

title: Numerical investigation of the aerodynamic performance and wake evolution of a coaxial co-rotating dual-rotor wind turbine
Design and optimization of reheated supercritical CO2 cycle systems for thermal energy storage and discharge processes using a bisection method
Optimized multi-energy scheduling of gas–steam–power systems for metallurgical coking site: focusing on gas holder regulation characteristics
Reinforcement learning energy management strategy for HEVs based on structure-aware temporal prediction and information bridge mechanism
Landfill gas-to-energy in Colombia: A multicriteria assessment of electricity generation potential, costs, and emissions reduction
System-level techno-economic analysis of hydrogen-fuelled genset internal combustion engines with exhaust-driven power recovery
abstract: Hydrogen-fuelled internal combustion engines (H 2 -ICEs) are increasingly considered as transitional low-carbon power technologies, yet their deployment is limited by reduced efficiency and high electricity costs under open-cycle operation. This study presents a unified thermodynamic and techno-economic comparison of gasoline, open-cycle hydrogen, and waste-heat-recovery-integrated H 2 -ICE generator systems using an ASPEN-based process simulation framework. At the highest stable equivalence ratios examined (φ = 1.045 for gasoline and φ = 0.857 for hydrogen), the open-cycle H 2 -ICE exhibits a 17.5 % lower brake thermal efficiency than gasoline, at 33.4 % versus 40.5 %. To mitigate this penalty, an exhaust-mounted electric turbogenerator (ETG) coupled with a proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyser is integrated to recover exhaust energy and enable in-situ hydrogen regeneration. When system performance is evaluated based on the combined engine brake and recovered electrical output, the integrated H 2 -ICE with waste heat recovery achieves apparent extended system-level energy utilisation factors of 54.4 % using ASPEN simulations and 52.3 % based on theoretical analysis. Techno-economic analysis under defined operating conditions of 5 h day −1 and 365 days year −1 shows that open-cycle hydrogen increases the levelised cost of electricity by approximately 34 % for grey hydrogen and more than 400 % for green hydrogen relative to gasoline, whereas waste heat recovery reduces the grey hydrogen LCOE to 0.727 MYR kWh −1 . This corresponds to reductions of 39.4 % relative to open-cycle hydrogen and 18.6 % relative to gasoline. Overall, the results demonstrate that the viability of hydrogen ICEs is governed by system-level energy recovery and integration rather than standalone engine efficiency, highlighting the thermodynamic potential of waste-heat-recovery-integrated H 2 -ICEs as a transitional low-carbon stationary power concept under favourable integration and component cost assumptions.

title: Integrated methane production and liquefaction via vanadium-chlorine thermochemical cycle and vacuum swing adsorption process
abstract: The conversion of carbon dioxide into synthetic fuels using low-carbon hydrogen has attracted attention as a promising strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and supporting sustainable energy systems. In this study, an integrated process for carbon capture, hydrogen production, methane synthesis, and its liquefaction is developed and evaluated. The proposed system combines a vanadium-chlorine thermochemical cycle for hydrogen production, a vacuum swing adsorption process for carbon capture, catalytic methane synthesis, and methane liquefaction in a heat-integrated framework that recovers and reuses thermal energy to reduce external energy demand. The results demonstrate that effective heat integration enhances overall system performance, increasing the energy efficiency from 39.3% to 58.8% and the exergy efficiency from 57.8% to 69.3%. Economic analysis reveals a levelized production cost of 23.19 $/million Btu, a net annual profit of 2.153 million $, and a payback period of 4.95 years. Sensitivity analysis identifies the adsorption unit, methanation reactor, and thermochemical hydrogen production cycle as the key subsystems governing process performance. Increasing carbon dioxide capture capacity raises the energy and exergy efficiencies to 58.8% and 69.3%, respectively, while reducing the methanation reactor temperature increases these values to 59.0% and 70.5%, respectively. Furthermore, increasing hydrogen availability enhances methane production until the stoichiometric requirement of the methanation reactor is satisfied, whereas methanation pressure has only a minor influence on overall system performance. The proposed system demonstrates promising thermodynamic and economic performance for carbon utilization and low-carbon fuel production, although further improvements are needed to compete with conventional liquefied natural gas technologies.

title: Experimentally validated dynamic modeling and seasonal solar radiation adaptability of PEM electrolyzers for renewable hydrogen production
abstract: To address the challenges of accurately predicting the dynamic behavior of proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzers under fluctuating renewable energy inputs and the high cost of long-term experiments, this paper develops and validates a PEM dynamic model via the experimental and simulation combined approach to. A voltage model with current density and temperature as variables was established through static polarization curves and dynamic step/ramp load change experiments. The proposed model captures both electrical and thermal transient characteristics and is validated using a PEM electrolyzer experiment platform. The results agree well with the validation experiments, with a static mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0033 V, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.004 V, and a maximum dynamic temperature deviation below 0.5 °C. Subsequently, the developed model was applied to dynamic system simulations under representative seasonal conditions as well as an extreme low‑irradiance scenario. Seasonal comparison shows that summer achieves the highest average hydrogen production efficiency of 74.7 %, along with an average specific energy consumption (SEC) of 4.115 kWh/Nm3 and an average cell voltage of 1.72 V. Although autumn delivers the highest daily hydrogen production of 52.74 mol, winter exhibits a comparatively higher average hydrogen production efficiency (73.4 %) than both spring and autumn despite generating the lowest daily hydrogen output (34.71 mol). Under an extreme low-irradiance condition, hydrogen output falls to 12.2 mol, while the system continues to operate stably without shutdown or failure, exhibiting strong environmental adaptability. This synergistic method (experiment, modeling, validation, simulation) offers a reliable and computationally efficient tool for long-term performance assessment and operational optimization of PEM electrolyzer systems integrated with variable renewable energy sources.

title: Dynamic energy supply–demand matching of an integrated thermal management system for high-power pulsed lasers
Performance boosting of a thermoelectric generator via impinging jet array for flue gas heat harvesting from a super-adiabatic porous combustor
Effect of front partial shadings with different transmittances and areas on thermal and electrical performance of half-cell bifacial photovoltaic panel: An outdoor experiment
Comprehensive optimization of ammonia-enriched fueled CI engines via injector geometry matching
Ethanol steam reforming under engine exhaust-like conditions: energy recovery of reformate and coke-to-power integrated approach
abstract: Ethanol steam reforming (ESR) was evaluated as an on-board energy recovery strategy for internal combustion engines under engine exhaust-like conditions using a bench-scale reactor and two catalysts: a commercial Ni/Al₂O₃ catalyst promoted with CaO and K₂O, and a Co catalyst supported on sepiolite. Experiments were conducted between 300 and 600 °C, selected according to exhaust temperature ranges experimentally obtained in a medium-duty compression ignition (CI) engine, and at steam-to-ethanol (S/E) ratios from 3:1 to 13:1. The nickel catalyst showed the broadest and most robust operating window, achieving complete conversion above 400 °C and positive energy recovery over a wide temperature range, although with significant coke formation at intermediate temperatures (400–500 °C), especially at low S/E ratios. The cobalt catalyst exhibited lower activity but higher hydrogen selectivity and lower methane formation, with optimal performance concentrated above 500 °C and negligible coke under high steam conditions. Considering the additional energy recovered from coke gasification, overall energy recovery reached values of 1.17–1.20 under optimal conditions, confirming the viability of ESR coupled with exhaust waste heat. This integrated reforming–regeneration analysis highlights that moderate coke formation does not necessarily penalize the overall energy balance, provided that effective regeneration strategies are implemented. However, bench-scale operation also revealed progressive mechanical degradation of the catalyst bed, including erosion, fragmentation, and pulverization caused by repeated coke formation–regeneration cycles, leading to increased pressure drop and operability limitations.

title: Technical assessment of large-scale PCM packed beds for water-free gas turbine inlet air cooling and peak power enhancement
Process modelling of municipal solid waste gasification with non-thermal plasma tar-cracking unit for mass and energy recovery
abstract: Growing municipal solid waste generation continues to outpace conventional disposal methods, and while gasification can turn waste into a synthetic gas, tar formation limits this gas mainly to combustion. Non-thermal plasma tar cracking can remove tar, but it has mainly been demonstrated at bench scale, with limited investigation of its integration into waste gasification systems. It was hypothesised that linking a gasification flowsheet to a regression model of non-thermal plasma tar cracking would reveal the trade-off between syngas quality and energy demand. A process model combining waste gasification with a non-thermal plasma tar cracking unit, represented using a multilinear-regression surrogate derived from plasma simulations, was built and tested across six pathways. The flowsheet predicted a syngas of hydrogen (52.3 %), carbon monoxide (25.3 %), carbon dioxide (14.0 %), and methane (3.9 %), in agreement with previous work, and the regression model achieved species-dependent coefficients of determination of 66.94–94.66 %. Overall non-thermal plasma removed most tar but added 1.80–2.00 kW per kilogram of waste, favouring methanol synthesis and fuel cells over conventional power generation.

title: Data driven models for online tar monitoring in biomass gasification
abstract: Reliable real-time monitoring of tar concentration remains a major barrier to process control and downstream syngas utilization. While online tar measurement is often constrained by high system complexity and associated costs, data-driven soft sensors offer a feasible and efficient alternative. Existing approaches often treat tar concentration in its raw form, despite its highly skewed distribution, which can compromise model stability, generalization, and the physical reliability of soft-sensor predictions. This study proposes a data-driven soft-sensor pipeline for the online estimation of tar concentration, combining domain-specific feature engineering, target-variable transformation, and deployment-oriented latency assessment across 11 ML algorithms, one DL model, and a Stacking Regressor ensemble, using a dataset comprising 221 literature-derived experimental records. The proposed pipeline systematically assesses the impact of four target variable transformations (logarithmic, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, and untransformed raw data). Results demonstrate that target variable transformation is crucial for model stabilization and generalization. On the independent test set, the Stacking Regressor model coupled gradient and categorical boosting regressors achieves the best predictive performance (R 2 = 0.85, RMSE = 4.06 g/Nm 3 ). Similarly, the single categorical boosting regressor coupled with Box-Cox transformation proves to be a robust alternative (R 2 = 0.83). In addition, all top-performing models met the 1 Hz real-time monitoring constraint, indicating the feasibility of the proposed pipeline for soft-sensor deployment in biomass gasification systems. Overall, the findings show that boosting and ensemble nonlinear models combined with appropriate target-variable transformation offer a better balance between accuracy, generalization, and computational feasibility than more complex architectures, highlighting their potential for use as soft sensors for real-time tar monitoring in biomass gasification systems.

title: Decarbonizing European refineries: GHG accounting framework and potential assessment for co-processed biofuels
abstract: Co-processing of biogenic feedstocks in existing crude oil refineries is a promising, near-term option to decarbonize transport fuels by using existing fossil conversion infrastructure. This study quantifies the life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of co-processed biofuels under an average European refinery configuration, using a policy-compliant approach consistent with the EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED), which has been integrated with a refinery-wide mass and energy balance model. Four case studies were selected: used cooking oil (UCO) co-processing in hydrotreating (HT) and hydrocracking (HC) conversion routes, and fast pyrolysis oil (FPO) and stabilized/hydrotreated pyrolysis oil (SPO/HDO) co-processing in fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) conversion pathways. Biogenic feed shares of 5–20 wt% at the conversion unit inlet were modelled, together with a full mass and energy balance for all pathways, derived to develop a comprehensive LCI for each pathway. Considered products comprised biogenic diesel, biogenic gasoline and biogenic kerosene. All pathways achieved substantial GHG savings relative to fossil fuels, with carbon intensities ranging from 3.9 to 25.8 g CO 2 e MJ −1 and GHG emissions savings of 73–96 %, thus remaining well above the 65 % RED minimum GHG emissions reduction threshold. UCO hydroprocessing delivered the lowest carbon intensities, while FCC pathways showed higher values, due to lower liquid-fuel yields and greater upstream burdens. Extrapolating the representative case-study yields to the entire EU refining system, a theoretical biofuel potential of up to 13.9 Mt y −1 at 5 % bio-share at conversion unit inlet is estimated.

title: Balanced use of recuperator in an MGT-powered eVTOL for extending cruise-stage flight time
abstract: Although recuperators are not widely used in micro gas turbines for aircraft due to the concern of added weight, modern design and manufacturing technologies are able to make recuperators both compact and efficient, which makes the situation worth another assessment. The presented research systematically investigates the pros and cons of adopting a recuperative micro gas turbine for eVTOL applications. The research takes a 30 kW micro gas turbine power chain as an example and develops a system model consisting of the gas turbine, a recuperator, the weight and loading of the eVTOL, propellers and motors. A Pareto-based optimisation strategy is developed to identify the flight-time-optimal balance between the mass of the recuperator and the mass of the fuel under different cruise-speed and payload conditions. Under the long-duration forward-flight conditions considered, compared with the simple-cycle configuration in which the recuperator mass is replaced by an equal mass of fuel, the optimised recuperated configuration increases the calculated flight time by approximately 10–15 % over a broad low-payload range, with a maximum absolute gain of about 1.3 h. These findings demonstrate that recuperated micro gas turbines have clear advantages over simple-cycle micro gas turbines for some eVTOL applications. A well-balanced recuperator can therefore extend the flight time while reducing fuel consumption and direct CO 2 emissions under favourable operating conditions.

title: Improved holistic performance of Carnot battery using compressed air energy storage technology: comprehensive optimization, assessment and performance robustness evaluation
Performance investigation of a novel two-stage compression heat pump system for multi-level waste heat utilization
abstract: High-temperature heat pumps can upgrade low-grade industrial waste heat but face multi-level heat sources and large temperature lifts. A two-stage compression heat pump with intermediate cooling (TSHP-IC) is proposed to combine staged heat absorption with two-stage compression, together with an enhanced internal-heat-exchanger configuration (TSHP-IC-IHX). A steady-state thermodynamic model is developed for low-GWP zeotropic mixtures, particularly R1234ze(Z)/R1336mzz(Z). At waste-heat-source temperatures of 85 and 55 °C and heating temperatures of 100–120 °C, the working fluids are independently optimized for the proposed systems, a cascade dual-heat-source heat pump (CHP-DHR), and a parallel single-stage heat pump (PSHP). At 100 °C, TSHP-IC achieves a COP of 4.15, 2.45 % and 4.72 % higher than CHP-DHR and PSHP, respectively. Its performance is comparable to CHP-DHR at 110 °C and 1.67 % lower at 120 °C. After configuration-specific composition optimization, TSHP-IC-IHX reaches a COP of 4.55 at 100 °C and exceeds the correspondingly optimized CHP-DHR-HIHX by 4.94 %–6.31 % throughout the investigated range. Matched diagnostic calculations show that the IHX increases compressor-inlet superheat, reduces pre-throttling enthalpy and flash-vapor fraction, and expands the feasible composition range. At the representative heating temperature of 110 °C, the IHX-assisted configuration at its selected composition exhibits approximately 33 % lower total exergy destruction and an exergy-efficiency increase from 0.66 to 0.76 relative to the selected TSHP-IC case. These results demonstrate that combining two-stage compression with internal heat recovery is effective for large-temperature-lift, multi-level industrial waste heat utilization.

title: A novel TPV-Brayton hybrid system for hypersonic vehicles: efficient conversion and utilization of waste heat to power
Impact and optimization of hierarchical infrastructure configuration for vehicle-to-grid profitability in multi-service electricity markets
Theoretical and experimental study of a pillow – Plate flat plate collector using air as heat transfer fluid
abstract: This work presents the theoretical and experimental analysis of a novel air – based flat plate collector using pillow – plate (PP) geometry. The proposed design aims to enhance the heat transfer when using air as heat transfer fluid. A prototype was tested under outdoor conditions for airflow rates between 50 and 350 L/min and three internal flow configurations (H, U and Z), and a steady – state model based on the Hottel – Whillier approach was developed and validated. Results on temperature pattern distribution show that airflow rate dominates thermal performance. Efficiency increases with flow rate, exceeding 55 % for the H configuration, while temperature rise decreases, reaching up to 35 °C at low flow rates, corresponding to normalized temperature – rise values (ΔT/ A c ) above 200 °C/m 2 at airflow rates close to 50 L/min. The U configuration provides more uniform thermal behaviour, whereas the H configuration achieves the highest efficiencies. In addition, the steady − state model reproduced the experimental results with deviations generally within ± 10 % at intermediate and high airflow rates. The PP – based collector demonstrates competitive performance compared to conventional systems, highlighting its potential for low – temperature industrial and heating, ventilation and air conditioning applications.

title: Dynamic heating performance of a direct absorption/storage solar collector-assisted dual-source heat pump system
Dual-heat source thermoelectric generator: analytical design and performance evaluation
Experimental evaluation of a passive solar still enhanced with date palm fiber pin-finned wicks: a 10-E analytical framework
Diurnal intermittent spray cooling strategies for rooftop photovoltaics: experimental evaluation and heat transfer insights
Continuous ageing trajectory representations across heterogeneous battery datasets: Knee analysis and protocol-held-out early-life prediction
abstract: Accurate assessment of lithium-ion battery ageing is complicated by cell-to-cell variability, heterogeneous cycling protocols, and limited transferability of data-driven predictors. This study develops a continuous ageing-trajectory framework in which coordinate-based multilayer perceptron (MLP) and sinusoidal representation network (SIREN) models represent state-of-health and voltage–capacity trajectories as differentiable functions of normalized trajectory coordinates. The framework combines continuous reconstruction, derivative-based knee descriptors, equivalent-full-cycle (EFC) harmonization, protocol-held-out early-life prediction, perturbation analysis, and conformal uncertainty quantification. Early-life prediction was evaluated in four protocol-held-out folds, repeated for three random seeds, using the first 𝑁 ∈ { 5 , 1 0 , 2 0 } available degradation observations rather than assuming that one observation represented one physical cycle. The pooled association between robust consensus knee location and the first crossing of the 80% SOH threshold was strong ( 𝑛 = 1 7 2 , Spearman 𝜌 S = 0 . 8 3 4 , 95% bootstrap CI [ 0 . 7 3 8 , 0 . 9 0 7 ] , Holm-adjusted 𝑝 = 3 . 3 6 × 1 ⁢ 0 − 4 5 ). Raw adapted cINR predictions exhibited substantial architecture- and window-dependent bias. A leakage-safe bias-corrected MLP-protocol blend achieved MAEs of 113.57, 107.79, and 112.82 EFC for 𝑁 = 5 , 10, and 20, respectively, compared with 116.66, 115.57, and 125.02 EFC for the protocol-median baseline. These numerical reductions were not statistically significant after multiplicity correction, although the blend significantly improved over raw MLP cINR predictions for 𝑁 = 5 and 𝑁 = 1 0 . Fold-external conformal intervals at the nominal 90% level attained empirical coverages of 90.3%, 91.0%, and 95.5%, but remained wide, reflecting substantial inter-cell uncertainty. Knee detection was comparatively stable under missing observations but sensitive to aggressive downsampling and measurement noise. The results support continuous trajectory representations as useful differentiable descriptors and components of calibrated hybrid predictors, but do not establish a uniform predictive advantage over a strong protocol-informed baseline.

title: Performance analysis and scheme evaluation of coal-fired power plant retrofit integrated with Carnot battery energy storage
Spectrally resolved finite‑element modelling of radiative cooling under real atmospheric conditions: validation and benchmarking framework
abstract: Passive daytime radiative cooling (PDRC) promises zero-energy thermal management, but reported performances vary across studies due to local atmospheric conditions and non-standard experimental configurations. A spectrally resolved finite-element model has been developed and validated for predicting 24 h thermal response under realistic outdoor conditions. The model couples wavelength-dependent material optical properties and sky emissivities derived from libRadtran using real atmospheric data. Validation against different outdoor measurements of nanoporous anodic aluminium oxide and cellulose-based radiative coolers under Madrid summer conditions yields a normalised mean bias error within ± 10 % and coefficient of variation of the root mean square error < 11 %, fulfilling ASHRAE Guideline 14–2014 (gold standard for the validation of thermal models). Parametric studies reveal that geometric and design parameters dominate over atmospheric variations, with temperature differences relative to aluminium up to 25 °C vs. ∼ 0.2 °C for realistic humidity and temperature variations, reaching peak daytime net cooling powers ∼ 120 W·m −2 . Cloudy conditions are included (a cloud optical depth of 1 reduces the daily cooling power by 26 %) and global portability to other regions and climates is demonstrated (e.g., a 56 % decrease in cooling power predicted from Madrid to Singapore). This framework facilitates PDRC climate-specific optimisation and supports benchmarking for real-world applications. Furthermore, an initial benchmarking framework is introduced to mitigate historical discrepancies in outdoor PDRC characterization. Ultimately, this framework lays the foundation for developing digital twins of PDRC systems, bridging the gap between nanoscale material properties and macroscale building energy simulations.

title: Dual-stage Sabatier reactor with differential thermal management and membrane-based methane upgrading for high-purity methane production
abstract: This study proposes a dual-stage Sabatier reactor with differential thermal management and evaluates its performance together with a membrane-based methane upgrading process through experimental and numerical analyses. To overcome the thermal instability and equilibrium limitations associated with single-stage reactor operation, the reaction process was spatially separated into kinetically and thermodynamically favorable regions. The proposed thermal management strategy moderated excessive temperature rise, stabilized the reaction zone, and suppressed CO formation. Under stoichiometric conditions (H 2 /CO 2 = 4.0), the dual-stage reactor achieved a methane yield of 89.8 ± 2.4% (mean ± standard deviation of triplicate runs), while operation at H 2 /CO 2 = 5.0 reduced the outlet CO 2 concentration to below the reporting threshold (<1 vol%) and increased the methane yield to 94.0 ± 1.6%. The reactor also exhibited improved thermal stability, with the maximum temperature limited to approximately 560 °C in the first stage and below 320 °C in the second stage. The gas permeation characteristics of a polysulfone hollow-fiber membrane were experimentally evaluated and used to develop a one-dimensional counter-current membrane model consistent with the flow arrangement of the module. Without fitting to the mixed-gas data, the model reproduced the measured stage-cut, methane purity, and methane recovery over the experimentally investigated range of feed compositions (H 2 /CO 2 = 3.0–5.0) and operating pressures (1–3 bar gauge). Process simulations using the experimentally assessed model projected that methane purity and recovery of at least 95% can be achieved simultaneously in a two-stage permeate-linked configuration while maintaining the feed side at 1 bar gauge and reducing the permeate pressure to approximately 0.20 bar absolute. The chemical conversion efficiency and system efficiency within the defined process boundary were determined to be 74.3 ± 2.0% and 69.8 ± 1.9%, respectively; the latter includes reactor heating, feed compression, and membrane-related vacuum/interstage and recycle compression. The findings provide useful design guidance for Sabatier-based systems relevant to in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) and terrestrial CO 2 methanation applications.

title: Assessment of PFI-SI, DISI, and PCC modes in ultra-lean hydrogen engines towards clean and efficient combustion
abstract: Hydrogen engines are designed to run at ultra-lean conditions to suppress knocking and nitrogen oxides (NOx). This study aims to systematically assess various types of combustion strategies in achieving ultra-lean combustion. To ensure high-fidelity modeling of ultra-lean hydrogen-air combustion, several important model developments were conducted. In particular, ultra-lean hydrogen flames exhibit increased propensities in wall quenching and pronounced diffusive-thermal (DT) instability. To accurately describe these characteristics in turbulent and high-pressure conditions, a comprehensive combustion model was developed to represent DT-turbulence interaction and flame quenching effects, along with an updated chemical kinetic mechanism with detailed NOx formation. The integrated models were validated against experiments from port-fuel injection (PFI), direct-injection spark-ignition (DISI), and pre-chamber combustion (PCC) configurations. Detailed analysis of simulation results revealed that, relative to the PFI mode, the DT effects are mitigated in DISI conditions due to mixture stratification, whereas stronger effects are observed in PCC operation. Neglecting DT effects in the PCC configuration leads to near-misfire behavior, primarily due to underpredicted combustion rates in the pre-chamber region. Moreover, neglecting flame quenching is found to yield an overprediction of wall heat transfer loss and underprediction of hydrogen slip, especially for the PCC mode. A comparative assessment of the three combustion modes under identical operating conditions indicates that PFI produces the lowest NOx emissions due to the more homogenous lean mixture burning, while PCC results in slightly higher NOx emissions due to elevated combustion temperatures. Nevertheless, comparable peak thermal efficiencies of approximately 47% are achieved across all three combustion modes.

title: Aligning cost and carbon goals in policy-constrained hydrogen refueling systems
Performance enhancement of solar stills using a passive wind-driven vibration mechanism: an experimental, machine learning, and multi-objective optimization study
Visualization study on gas–liquid two-phase evolution in PEMFC with water self-adaptive flow field: regulation mechanism of operating conditions
A three-stage adaptive energy management strategy for extended-range electric vehicles under real-world road conditions and driving style adaptation
A room-level control strategy for dynamic heat supply–demand matching in solar–air source heat pump hybrid heating systems
Comparative assessment of AGMD and VMD systems configured with flat sheet and hollow fibre membranes: an energy and exergy, thermo-economic, and environmental analysis
abstract: Membrane Distillation (MD) systems, particularly Air Gap Membrane Distillation (AGMD) and Vacuum Membrane Distillation (VMD) in Flat Sheet (FS) and Hollow Fibre (HF) configurations, demonstrate strong potential for freshwater production, Yet, there remains a lack of comparative studies evaluating their energy, exergy, economic and environmental performance under similar conditions. This study presents a comparative analysis of four MD systems under similar operating conditions: FS-AGMD, HF-AGMD, FS-VMD and HF-VMD, and considers their respective costs and operation in Western Australia. The analysis was performed for single-stage and multi-stage configurations of up to ten modules, both with and without Heat Recovery (HR), to enhance efficiency and reduce the Cost of Water (COW). These systems were assessed in terms of energy, exergy, cost and environmental impacts, with results showing that for an optimal number of modules, HF-VMD achieved the highest water production (0.84 m 3 .d −1 ), while FS-AGMD had the lowest (0.16 m 3 .d −1 ). Further, COW depended on the number of stages, and decreased with additional stages, reaching the lowest values with HR: 13.39 USD.m −3 (Eight-Stage HF-VMD), 18.26 $.m −3 (Seven-Stage FS-VMD), 34.15 $.m −3 (Five-Stage HF-AGMD), and 52.67 $.m −3 (Seven-Stage FS-AGMD). Our analysis shows that the COW of HF-VMD with HR can be reduced to 12.55 $.m −3 when the water production increases to 1 m 3 .d −1 . In addition, results indicate that HF-AGMD exhibits the least exergy destruction, whereas HF-VMD produces the highest CO 2 and NO x emissions. This multi-stage evaluation emphasises the influence of heat recovery on performance and cost-efficiency.

title: Photovoltaic power forecasting and anomaly detection: a comparative study of statistical, deep learning, and zero-shot foundation models on seven years of real plant data
abstract: Faults and gradual performance degradation in photovoltaic plants often remain undetected, causing energy losses and increasing maintenance costs. Selecting an appropriate forecasting model for residual-based anomaly detection requires understanding the relative contributions of model architecture and sensor availability; a question not yet addressed by systematic benchmarks on long-term real data. This paper presents a controlled two-phase benchmark based on seven years of real 15-minute PV production data from a grid-connected plant with two synchronised inverters. Four models are evaluated: a multiplicative Prophet model, a Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average model with exogenous regressors, a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory network, and Chronos-2, a zero-shot foundation model requiring no fine-tuning on plant-specific data. In Phase 1, models use only historical production data. In Phase 2, plane-of-array irradiance and module temperature are added as real-time covariates. With covariates, all models exceed R 2 = 0.97, enabling a shared three-stage anomaly detection pipeline to identify five operationally distinct fault categories, including inverter blackouts, partial faults, and snow accumulation. Across the test year, two confirmed fault events are identified: a total blackout with an estimated energy loss of 80 kWh and a partial fault with a loss of 21 kWh; the blackout is detected by all models. Zero-shot spatial transfer of the Prophet model to the second inverter achieves R 2 = 0.966, outperforming full retraining. Results show that covariate availability has a greater impact on forecast accuracy than model architecture itself. In covariate-rich settings, higher forecast accuracy corresponds to reduced anomaly detection sensitivity. The findings demonstrate that zero-shot foundation models are ready for deployment in PV plants lacking historical data, enabling scalable intelligent monitoring without upfront training.

title: Mechanism and mitigation of membrane-drying-induced local reversal in proton exchange membrane fuel cells through targeted hydrothermal regulation
A multi-domain coupled and multi-timescale commercial building energy model with hierarchical temperature control
Multi-zone phase change thermal management for accelerating hydrogen storage in LaNi5 alloy
A dimensionless dynamic similarity framework for solar process water heating systems with fully mixed thermal storage
Synthetic e-kerosene production from water and CO2 via a single-step RWGS-FT process: A techno-economic and global assessment
abstract: This study investigates the production of e-kerosene in the context of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) through direct CO 2 hydrogenation in a single-reactor Plug Flow Reactor (PFR) configuration, where CO 2 and renewable hydrogen are co-fed over potassium-promoted iron-based catalysts. Hydrogen is generated via proton exchange membrane (PEM) water electrolysis powered by renewable energy sources, enabling a fully renewable Power-to-Liquid (PtL) pathway for sustainable aviation fuel production. Within the reactor, simultaneous Reverse Water Gas Shift (RWGS) and Fischer–Tropsch (FT) reactions convert CO 2 into a synthetic crude enriched in kerosene-range hydrocarbons under operating conditions of 300 °C and 25 atm. Process simulation reveals that the Syn-Kerosene fraction is predominantly distributed within the C 8 –C 15 carbon-number range, with a pronounced maximum centered around C 9 –C 10 . In particular, Syn-Kerosene is primarily distributed between C 9 and C 13 , reaching peak selectivity values of approximately 0.21 at C 10 . Syn-Kerosene represents the dominant product fraction, achieving the highest single mass yield of 33.0 %. To improve efficiency, process optimizations are implemented to minimize energy and raw material consumption and maximize heat recovery and turbine-based power integration. Despite these optimizations, the PEM electrolyzer accounts for approximately 35 % of the total capital investment and 49 % of the total operating costs. A comprehensive techno-economic assessment is conducted through discounted cash-flow analysis and Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate long-term profitability and investment risk under varying assumptions of fixed capital cost, raw material costs, and product prices. Probabilistic distributions of Net Present Value (NPV), Discounted Cash Flow Rate of Return (DCFROR), and Discounted Payback Period (DPBP) are generated for production capacities ranging from 0.472 to 100 kt/y, highlighting the strong influence of process scale on economic feasibility. Finally, a global applicability analysis is performed to identify regions with favorable conditions for large-scale deployment of the technology. Within Europe, Nordic countries, such as Norway and Sweden, exhibit the highest suitability scores due to their high availability of renewable and low-carbon electricity relative to carbon emissions. The results demonstrate the techno-economic feasibility and limitations of direct FT-CO 2 hydrogenation as a scalable pathway for the production of e-kerosene in the aviation sector. Unlike previous analyses of CO 2 hydrogenation to e-kerosene based on individual case studies, the novelty of this work lies in an integrated assessment of the direct RWGS–FT process, combining reactor design and operating-condition optimization with process integration, techno-economic analysis, scale-up analysis, and regional assessment of renewable-electricity availability, thereby addressing the literature gap arising from the separate consideration of these aspects.

title: Techno–economic optimisation of hydrogen geological storage in UK depleted gas reservoirs
abstract: Long-duration energy storage is becoming critical in the UK to manage renewable intermittency, prolonged low-generation periods, and energy curtailment. Depleted natural gas reservoirs offer a promising option for large-scale underground hydrogen storage because of their substantial capacities, established containment, and well-characterised geology. However, a systematic assessment linking reservoir-scale behaviour to cost-optimal UK storage portfolios remains lacking. Here, we formulate a cost-aware portfolio optimisation framework that combines compositional reservoir simulations, surrogate modelling, and techno-economic optimisation across representative UK reservoir properties and operating conditions. The simulations identify permeability, porosity, reservoir pressure, and density contrast between H 2 and cushion gas as the dominant controls on recovery, while injection rate and cycle duration have comparatively lower influence. These results support a high-accuracy surrogate model that enables rapid evaluation of feasible storage configurations for delivery requirements from 5 to 200 TWh. By linking reservoir-dependent recovery to H 2 losses, purification, and storage-system costs, the framework determines cost-optimal combinations of depleted gas reservoirs and operating strategies. The optimised portfolios produce long-term levelised storage costs of approximately 30–60 $ MWh −1 . Higher delivery requirements generally increase costs because fewer annual cycles are available to distribute infrastructure and inventory costs. When purification costs approach H 2 production costs, cushion-gas ratios of 2–4 are favoured for the 5 TWh case, decreasing to 0–1 for requirements of 100 TWh and above; inexpensive purification shifts the preferred ratio towards zero. Across scenarios, selected reservoirs consistently exhibit permeabilities of 10–30 mD, porosities of 0.10–0.15, and pressures of 250–300 bar, conditions that reduce buoyant mixing while maintaining practical deliverability.

title: Power output prediction of a coastline-integrated linear oscillating water column array with periodic wave-guiding structures in regular and irregular waves
Thermodynamic performance’s analysis of a hybrid thermal-compressor-thermochemical sorption processes using ammoniated salts for cold production
TPMS metallic porous skeleton-enhanced heat transfer characteristics of solid–liquid phase change materials for thermal energy storage applications
abstract: Latent heat thermal energy storage using phase change materials (PCMs) is limited by the low thermal conductivity of organic PCMs. To enhance heat transfer while retaining latent-heat capacity, five triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) metallic skeleton topologies with uniform, positive-gradient, and reverse-gradient porosity distributions were embedded in paraffin and tested under side- and bottom-heating conditions. Experiments quantified the propagation of the 37.2 °C DSC melting-onset threshold using point-to-point transit time, onset-threshold coverage time, threshold-front distance, and apparent onset-threshold-covered area fraction. Numerical validation and hypothetical design analyses used I-WP as the representative topology to examine the roles of skeleton conduction and natural convection. Under side heating, positive-gradient structures generally showed the best threshold-based heat-transfer performance. The positive-gradient Primitive skeleton reduced the point-1-to-point-5 onset-threshold transit time by 68.7%. Under bottom heating, threshold-front morphology and stage-wise propagation indicated a stronger contribution of buoyancy-driven natural convection in regions farther from the heat source. For I-WP, the model reasonably reproduced the experimental threshold-front evolution and relative performance of the three porosity distributions. Further simulations showed that the positive-gradient I-WP design reduced the energy-storage completion time by 43.8% relative to the reverse-gradient design. These results demonstrate that TPMS topology and porosity gradients can be tailored to improve high-rate thermal-energy storage.

An integrated framework for PEMFC state prediction and BOP fault diagnosis based on inter-feature association rules
Breaking the dimensionality curse in floating offshore wind farms: A spatiotemporal decoupled reduced-order modeling framework
Physics-constrained adversarial Transformer for abnormal data identification and reconstruction in large-scale photovoltaic power plants

Vanadium extraction tailings based composite phase change materials: Preparation and pore-scale simulation for packed-bed thermal energy storage systems
Multi-objective optimal design of a Carnot battery system based on entropy weight–TOPSIS
abstract: Carnot battery systems have gained widespread attention due to their potential applications in energy storage, and round-trip efficiency has become a primary research focus. However, system performance is not only determined by the thermodynamic cycle itself, but is also significantly influenced by storage capacity configuration, which involves complex trade-offs among utilization, reliability, and economic performance.To achieve optimal design under multiple performance criteria, this study proposes a multi-objective optimization framework based on the entropy weight method and TOPSIS for storage capacity configuration in Carnot battery systems. A dynamic model integrating a heat pump, thermal storage tank, and organic Rankine cycle is developed using Simulink. Key performance indicators, including storage utilization, peak-shaving capability, system reliability, and economic performance, are evaluated under different peak-shaving limit conditions.The results indicate that storage capacity plays a dominant role in system performance and exhibits strong coupling among multiple indicators. The optimal storage capacity decreases significantly from approximately 63% to 20% as the peak-shaving limit increases from 550 kW to 675 kW. The proposed method avoids over- or under-sizing of storage capacity and achieves a balance among multiple performance objectives, providing a reliable basis for system design and operation.

title: An experimental approach to study simultaneous usage of nanomaterials and pin-fins on the behavior of hybrid PCMs for chipset cooling and energy storage applications
Experimental and numerical study of a bio-methane heavy-duty engine equipped with a pre-chamber ignition system: a focus on flame kernel development and combustion process under lean conditions
abstract: In this work, in-depth experimental and numerical analyses are carried out on a single-cylinder bio-methane heavy-duty spark ignition engine, mounting a passive pre-chamber, to investigate the flame kernel formation, the combustion process and the overall performance. In the first stage, an extensive experimental activity is performed on the examined engine. Measurements are carried out in several engine operating points, exploring lean mixture conditions up to the lean burn limit and recording global engine parameters, combustion indicators, in-cylinder pressure traces and emissions. A 0D/1D engine model, integrated with user-coded phenomenological sub-models of flame kernel, turbulent combustion and emissions, is developed and combustion is properly tuned referring to the experimental stoichiometric points. A physics-based correlation of flame kernel duration for air/bio-methane charge is identified to forecast the kernel formation time at the spark event, which is a challenging task in presence of diluted mixtures and variable in-cylinder thermodynamic conditions. Flame kernel formation time predicted by the correlation considers the dependencies on pressure, unburned temperature, equivalence ratio and residual gas content of the air/fuel mixture. The proposed numerical approach demonstrates that a reliable prediction of the kernel duration remarkably improves the simulation of burn rates and pressure traces in the main chamber, especially under high mixture dilutions. The 0D/1D model accounting for the kernel formation satisfactorily replicates the main engine performance, including net Indicated mean effective pressure and Indicated specific fuel consumption with maximum absolute errors of 1.8% and 4%, respectively; main gaseous emissions (nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons) are reproduced with an overall acceptable accuracy; greater errors are observed only at high load, with absolute experimental/numerical deviations of about 200 ppm for nitrogen oxides and slightly greater than 400 ppm for carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons.

title: In-situ analysis of reaction distributions in a solid oxide cell for H2O/CO2 co-electrolysis using segmented electrodes
abstract: The internal reaction behavior of solid oxide electrolysis cell (SOEC) co-electrolysis is strongly influenced by coupled electrochemical and chemical reactions, yet its local characteristics remain insufficiently understood. In this study, a planar Ni–YSZ|YSZ|GDC|LSC SOEC with a three-segment oxygen electrode was used to measure local current and temperature, outlet gas composition, and electrochemical impedance under different H 2 O/CO 2 feed ratios at 650 °C. Increasing the CO 2 fraction lowers the current density and increases the area-specific resistance. Under steam-containing conditions, the local current density decreases from the upstream to the downstream segment due to reactant consumption. However, under the 10%H 2 –60%CO 2 –30%N 2 condition, the midstream current density exceeds the upstream value. Local impedance analysis indicates that this non-monotonic behavior is associated with lower ion-conduction-related and gas-diffusion/conversion resistances in the midstream region. For steam-containing feeds, temperature measurements show a shift from endothermic to exothermic around the theoretical thermoneutral voltages with increasing voltage, while the apparent thermoneutral voltage under the 10%H 2 –60%CO 2 –30%N 2 condition is significantly lower than the theoretical value, indicating additional thermal effects from coupled chemical reactions. Outlet gas analysis reveals that the reverse water–gas shift (RWGS) reaction occurs without electrolysis. Post-test scanning electron microscopy and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy characterization of the disassembled cell identifies carbon deposits in the fuel electrode. These findings indicate that the RWGS reaction and carbon deposition reaction are possible contributors to the local variations in temperature and current density. The results provide local experimental evidence for understanding internal heterogeneity in SOEC co-electrolysis and for validating multiphysics models.

title: Enhancement of in-cylinder flow and combustion in a methane port injection engine by introducing gasoline direct injection
Structural optimization and optical-thermal performance of molten salt receivers based on the reabsorption effect
Design characteristics and engineering feasibility of small-scale refrigeration centrifugal compressors
Experimentally calibrated turbulence correction of tesla-turbine laminar model and its effect on ORC design selection

Performance and modeling of ejectors in transcritical CO2 heat pump systems for electric vehicles considering bubble nucleation and growth
abstract: Developing electric vehicles (EVs) serves as a critical initiative to alleviate energy shortages and safeguard the ecological environment, within which high-efficiency integrated thermal management stands out as a paramount research focus, making transcritical CO 2 ejector heat pump systems a mainstream trend in thermal management architectures. However, the internal non-equilibrium phase change within the ejector employed to mitigate throttling losses and recover expansion work, as well as the underlying mechanisms influenced by geometric parameters, remain obscure. A numerical model was established and experimentally validated for a two-phase carbon dioxide ejector considering cavitation-evaporation and condensation effects, focusing on investigating its internal microscopic bubble nucleation and growth and further extending to macroscopic thermodynamic predictions. Through model capturing, with the increase of the ejector mixing chamber diameter, the axial range of the high-speed and low-temperature core region is shortened during shock wave oscillations. The mixing chamber isentropic efficiency exhibits an identical variation trend to the entrainment ratio, both peaking at 3.2 mm with maximum values of 0.9271 and 0.8111, respectively, before showing a downward trend. Furthermore, with the enlargement of the primary nozzle diverging angle, bubble growth accelerates, leading to an increase in the bubble number density. The throat isentropic efficiency shares a consistent variation rule with the entrainment ratio, reaching maximums of 0.9401 and 0.6704 at 2° divergent angle, exhibiting a non-linear pattern of initially increasing and then decreasing. Finally, the data acquired by the model are utilized to fit a one-dimensional thermodynamic isentropic efficiency prediction formula for optimizing the ejector modeling parameters.

title: Thermodynamic and economic analysis of a carbon dioxide-mediated propane oxidative dehydrogenation process for propylene and syngas with hierarchical waste heat recovery
Convection-driven divergence between apparent and operational efficiency in thermogalvanic cells
Experimental investigation on pre-chamber fuel system design and topology
Development of an innovative latent heat thermal energy storage prototype through analytical, numerical, and experimental modelling
abstract: Advancing energy efficiency is essential for mitigating the impact of the maritime sector on fuel consumption and global greenhouse gas emissions. Thermal energy storage systems can significantly enhance vessel energy performance by minimising energy losses, stabilising fluctuations in thermal energy supply, and efficiently harvesting intermittent waste heat sources. This research presents the design, modelling, and preliminary experimental assessment of a latent heat thermal energy storage (LHTES) prototype incorporating pillow plates and a phase change material (PCM). The device comprises a bundle of pillow plates featuring linear and spot internal welds to create distinct pathways for the heat transfer fluid and a dimpled surface to enhance heat exchange. The pillow plates are arranged in parallel stacks, vertically aligned along their shorter axis, enclosed in a tank with a lid, and surrounded by PCM as the energy storage medium. A parametric study was conducted with an analytical model to evaluate the impact of the main geometric and operational parameters on the performance of LHTES devices and to define the prototype specifications. These findings were further refined through three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and the predictions of both models were compared. Preliminary experiments were performed on a partially filled configuration of the device to verify the hydraulic and thermal operation of the assembled prototype within the operating limits of the available test rig. The combined analytical and CFD results provide a detailed understanding of the fluid dynamic and thermodynamic behaviour of the final configuration, containing the complete amount of PCM, under the design operating conditions. The developed prototype has an energy storage capacity of 26.51 kWh, an energy storage density of 54.76 kWh/m 3 , an average thermal power of 2.82 kW, and a mass of approximately 710 kg overall.

title: Toward economical and carbon-negative green hydrogen: An integrated process design of ammonia autothermal reforming with solid oxide fuel cell
Thermal-hydraulic enhancement of immersion-cooled cylindrical lithium-ion battery modules using end-face copper layers and arc-shaped inlet deflectors
Peer-to-peer energy sharing and storage strategies for potential positive energy Districts: A case study of a purely commercial district
abstract: Commercial districts account for a substantial share of urban electricity demand and greenhouse gas emissions, yet they remain underrepresented in Positive Energy District research, which predominantly focuses on residential or mixed-use areas. This study investigates to what extent a purely commercial district can be a potential positive energy district, including different energy management strategies such as peer-to-peer energy exchanges and storage integration. A hybrid modelling framework combining optimization-based decision variables with rule-based operational strategies is developed and applied to Centro Sicilia, a real-world commercial district composed of eleven heterogeneous buildings, including retail stores, a shopping mall, a cinema and a warehouse, in Catania, Sicily. A total of 122 scenarios are simulated, ranging from a baseline configuration to progressively integrated peer-to-peer exchanges, stationary battery systems, and electric vehicle storage. Results show that PV generation alone can theoretically cover up to 62 % of district electricity demand, but, of this amount, only 37 % is directly self-consumed due to temporal mismatches. Peer-to-peer and storages are thus investigated in terms of their capability to increase renewable energy penetration and impacting on grid import and export. From the results, stationary batteries emerge as the most effective flexibility resources, while electric vehicles provide a complementary but limited contribution. The findings demonstrate that commercial districts can support the extension of the positive energy district concept to high-demand urban contexts.

title: Thermodynamic analysis of a solar-powered hybrid polygeneration system using linear fresnel reflectors for multi-energy production
Editorial Board
Compact thermoelectric generators for autonomous low-power applications: sub-zero to +50 °C characterization and converter-loaded activation thresholds
abstract: Autonomous low-power electronics, including IoT sensor nodes, wireless environmental monitors, and distributed data-acquisition devices, require sustainable power that eliminates periodic battery replacement. Thermoelectric generators (TEGs) harvest energy continuously from ambient temperature differentials, yet manufacturer datasheets report performance only at large differentials (ΔT ≥ 50 °C) and open-circuit conditions, neither reflecting realistic deployment. Systematic characterization of small-form-factor commercial modules across low and sub-zero ΔT, and under realistic loaded operating points, remains limited.This study investigates six commercial compact bismuth telluride TEG modules (11 × 11 mm to 30 × 30 mm) across −15 °C to +50 °C. A custom Peltier-based test bench with a low-cost cooling-spray protocol enabled cold-side temperatures down to −15 °C without climate-chamber facilities. All modules show highly linear voltage–differential behaviour (R² = 0.961–0.990), with effective Seebeck coefficients of 3.19–7.31 mV/K, and deliver 0.39–1.81 mW at a 20 °C differential. Counterintuitively, the 19 × 19 mm module is outperformed by the smaller 15 × 15 mm module, traced to its higher internal resistance offsetting the added thermocouples; footprint area alone is not a reliable selection criterion.A key practical finding is that TEG terminal voltage under converter load falls 15–39 % below its open-circuit value at activation, scaling with internal resistance (r = 0.98). This links a standard datasheet parameter to realistic cold-start behaviour. Under ultra-low-voltage converter loading, all modules cold-start at ΔT ≤ 6.8 °C, the best near 4.5 °C. The results give validated design guidelines and application-specific module recommendations for autonomous low-power energy harvesting.

title: Numerical analyses into carbon circularity through integrated biomass gasification and electrochemical CO2 conversion to formic acid
abstract: The present study proposes an integrated gasification-electrochemical CO 2 reduction system for the co-production of syngas and formic acid, hence, reducing CO 2 emissions and promoting carbon circularity. Unlike the conventional gasification systems which focus primarily on syngas production, the proposed framework integrates downstream electrochemical recycling for the produced gas to convert the CO 2 into formic acid, providing additional carbon utilisation. A 2D Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) integrated model composed of two separate sub models (gasification and electrochemical) was established. The model investigated the influence of equivalence ratio (ER) on key performance parameters including lower heating value (LHV), H 2 production, CO 2 reduction, formic acid formation, gasification and carbon conversion efficiencies. In addition, a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) analysis was conducted to select the optimum working conditions. Based on the MCDM, an ER of 0.3 achieved the highest ranking. Compared to the stand-alone systems, the integrated system working under the suggested optimum ER produced lower CO 2 emissions by 27 vol%, higher formic acid by 31.7 wt%, higher H 2 production by 8.6 vol%, and higher gasification efficiency by 8.5 %. As a result, system integration significantly enhanced the overall process performance and improved fuel quality and energy recovery. The results indicate improvements in carbon utilisation and formic acid formation, however, before studying system scale-up and industrial deployment, some challenges must be addressed. This includes produced gas cleaning, renewable electricity requirements, electrochemical systems scaling, and economic and environmental viability studies.

title: Techno-economic assessment of hybrid solar spectral-splitting PV–thermal green hydrogen production systems
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive techno-economic assessment of a spectral-splitting photovoltaic-thermal hydrogen system across diverse climatic zones in Karlsruhe, Barcelona, Cairo and Dunhuang. By integrating optical-thermal simulations with an economic model, the analysis quantifies the impact of geography and tracking strategies on techno-economic performance. Results demonstrate a peak annual solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of around 20 % in high-irradiance regions like Cairo; specifically, while Cairo achieved the highest summer production yields, Dunhuang exhibited a unique profile that mitigates seasonal fluctuations, resulting in comparatively uniform hydrogen production throughout the year. The comparative analysis demonstrates that the substantial gain in hydrogen yield from dual axis tracking outweighs the incremental hardware costs. This establishes dual axis tracking as the economic optimum, reducing the levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) to 6.0 €/kg, approximately 9.6 % lower than the single axis baseline. Furthermore, Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis confirms that deploying the system in high-irradiance sites significantly compresses investment risk. Under hydrogen-only revenue situations, the discounted payback time (PBT) is around 6 years for dual axis configurations in Cairo and Dunhuang, while commercial valorisation of the oxygen byproduct accelerates capital recovery, reducing the PBT to around 5 years in Cairo.

title: Techno-economic assessments of a novel solar PV/T system with micro-channel heat pipe
Performance assessment of thermally integrated Carnot Batteries: limitations of conventional metrics and definition of a differential Round-Trip Efficiency
Global economic and environmental trade-offs of power-to-liquid fuels
abstract: Power-to-liquid (PtL) fuels are carbon-based liquid fuels made from hydrogen and carbon dioxide that can substitute fossil fuels in hard-to-electrify mobility sectors, particularly aviation and maritime transport, but their climate benefits depend strongly on how hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and electricity are supplied. Here, we assess global economic and environmental trade-offs for three PtL pathways: power-to-methanol, methanol-to-jet synthetic kerosene, and Fischer-Tropsch synthetic kerosene. We develop a high-resolution, spatially explicit framework that combines energy system optimization, techno-economic and prospective life cycle assessment. Low production costs and low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are often geographically misaligned today: renewable-rich regions such as North Africa, southern South America, and the Iberian Islands offer low-cost opportunities, whereas low-GHG grid-connected production is concentrated in regions with low-carbon power systems, such as Canada and northern Europe. Grid-connected production can be cost-effective but loses its climate advantage in carbon-intensive power systems, whereas off-grid renewable production delivers the lowest emissions at a cost premium. Configurations that combine grid electricity with dedicated renewables weaken this trade-off but remain sensitive to residual grid carbon intensity. For synthetic kerosene, Fischer-Tropsch routes are generally less GHG-intensive than methanol-to-jet routes under comparable electricity supply. Carbon pricing, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandates, and fossil-fuel price volatility can narrow the cost gap, but mainly for configurations with low well-to-wake emissions. PtL deployment should therefore be guided by electricity supply, regional siting, and full life cycle impacts rather than fuel labels alone.

title: Design and experimental validation of a beam-splitting and light-guiding solar concentrator for photovoltaic-thermal applications
abstract: This work presents the design, modelling and experimental validation of a high-concentrating beam-splitting and light-guiding solar concentrator developed within the SolDAC project framework. The architecture combines a linear Fresnel reflector (18.6 × ) with optimised free-form secondary optical elements (SOEs) (31.8 × ), reaching a global geometric concentration of 591 × . The SOEs integrate a circulating deionised water-filled cavity that performs spectral splitting and heat extraction while transforming the line focus into a light guiding-compatible point focus. Ray-tracing simulations show a global optical efficiency of ∼ 55%, accounting for reflection losses, transmission through the SOEs and absorption in the liquid cavity. The integrated system exhibits a tracking acceptance angle of ± 0.4°, consistent with high-concentration optics. Irradiance non-uniformity at the SOE exit is mitigated through a kaleidoscopic homogeniser to ensure stable photovoltaic operation. Experimental measurements on a full-scale prototype confirm the main optical trends provided by the design model, including the irradiance distribution at the Fresnel focus, the spectral transmission of the secondary receiver and the system-level optical performance. The proposed architecture demonstrates the feasibility of integrating high-concentration optics, liquid spectral splitting and light guiding into a single configuration intended for future CPVT (concentrating photovoltaic–thermal) systems for solar-driven CO 2 capture and conversion.

Techno-economic and environmental assessment of coal co-gasification with alternative carbon sources and CO2 capture and co-utilization for sustainable syngas production
abstract: Syngas derived from coal gasification is an important resource for chemicals and fuels production globally. However, extensive use of coal emits large volumes of CO 2 and other pollutants to the environment. Conversely, alternatives such as natural gas, biogas, purified biomethane, and captured CO 2 present cleaner methods for transitioning to sustainable energy. This study conducted a techno-economic and environmental assessment of integrated gasification pathways to determine the cost and environmental optimal performances. One conventional coal gasification and seven alternative co-gasification steady-state process models were developed and simulated in Aspen Plus® v14. A full factorial design was used to investigate the impact of feedstock blending ratios and CO 2 recycle fraction on greenhouse gas emissions and syngas minimum selling price. The effects of plausible future green hydrogen prices and carbon taxation on the syngas minimum selling price were also evaluated. Co-gasification of coal and natural gas in a fixed-bed gasifier, with downstream CO 2 capture and utilization, demonstrated the best transitional potential, achieving a 25.4% lower syngas minimum selling price and lowering greenhouse gas emissions by 44.3% compared to the conventional base case. A syngas minimum selling price evolution analysis under green hydrogen and carbon tax future market conditions revealed that carbon taxation is the primary driver of economic convergence between coal‑only and alternative configurations. These results demonstrated that coal–methane co-gasification with CO 2 utilisation offers a robust and economically strong pathway for the staged decarbonisation of coal-based syngas production.

title: Implementation of the myopic approach in the long-term energy planning and capacity expansion model; examination in a multizonal case
abstract: Long-term optimisation of the energy systems configuration often requires a lot of computational resources and time. Also, perfect foresight limits the robustness of the approach and uses static boundary conditions. To tackle these issues, the Highway to Renewable Energy Systems model is modified to enable both runs in perfect foresight and in the myopic approach for comparable cases. In this case, the modelling is done on the multizonal energy system encompassing Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The research compares the results obtained in the approach using perfect foresight and the myopic approach. The goal of the research is to display the differences in the outcomes when using these approaches. A 3-zone case was used to reduce the possible bias that could appear when using a single-zone case to make conclusions on the model behaviour. The results display the improvements in the modelling performance on the side of the hardware requirements as well as the time expenditure. The results show that the myopic approach changes the timing and composition of investments compared with perfect foresight. Total power-generation capacity additions are similar, with 73,98 GW in perfect foresight and 74,51 GW in the myopic run, meaning that the myopic case adds 0,53 GW more capacity. However, the composition differs: solar power additions decrease slightly from 48,59 GW in perfect foresight to 48,35 GW in myopic, while wind additions increase from 25,40 GW to 26,16 GW. The myopic pathway also shifts more investment into the later part of the horizon, especially 2045 and 2050. The differences are also visible in environmental impacts. Total carbon dioxide emissions over the model years increase from 95,12 Mt in perfect foresight to 112,67 Mt in myopic. These results indicate that the myopic approach can reduce the computational burden and better represent sequential planning, but it can also lead to higher system costs and emissions because decisions are made with limited foresight.

title: Energy, exergy and economic analysis of bioinspired wick solar desalination leaf
Local composition distribution of the zeotropic mixture in heat exchangers of auto-cascade refrigeration system: numerical modeling and experimental validation
A building-integrated earth-to-air heat exchanger coupled with a nanofluid-NEPCM-based spectral-splitting CPV/T system: Annual energy, exergy, and pareto performance analysis
Price makers in 100 % renewable power systems: shadow price formation through flexibility options, hydropower, and congestion in a multi-zonal model
abstract: The transition toward highly renewable energy systems requires large-scale deployment of new generation capacities while maintaining system reliability and economic efficiency. Since renewable resources are geographically unevenly distributed, cross-border electricity exchange and flexibility options gain in importance for balancing supply and demand. This research analyses the interaction between renewable generation deployment, cross-border electricity flows, and electricity price formation in interconnected energy systems. The analysis is performed using the Highway to Renewable Energy System model, which was expanded with a multizonal capability for this research. The analysed region comprises the interconnected systems of Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina. The results show that decarbonization is primarily achieved through large-scale deployment of variable renewable generation. By 2050, total wind and solar capacity increases 11,23-fold compared with 2025 values. Specifically, solar and wind capacities increase 13,3-fold and 6,7-fold, respectively. Shadow-price analysis of the electricity-balance constraint indicates a structural shift in price formation. Thermal power plants dominate marginal pricing in the early years, whereas flexibility technologies and cross-border electricity exchanges increasingly determine prices in later periods. In some systems, dammed hydropower also becomes a price-setting technology by reflecting the opportunity cost of not generating during periods with higher electricity prices. The increasing share of renewable generation also leads to zero or negative price hours with approximately 17 % of annual hours in some systems. Average electricity prices decline to about 20 EUR/MWh by 2050. These findings highlight the growing importance of flexibility technologies, storage, and cross-border balancing mechanisms in highly renewable and interconnected electricity systems.

Techno-economic optimisation of multi-sector coupled energy systems: A 1 GW electrolyser case study in Esbjerg, Denmark
abstract: The study demonstrated the organisational, technical, and economic aspectsof a multi-sector coupled energy system. A 1 GW electrolyser was coupledto an existing urban energy system in Denmark (Esbjerg) via pathways foroffloading excess heat to the district heating and district cooling networks,while maintaining thermal conditions. A novel methodology for sector couplingwas introduced, and a techno-economic mixed-integer linear programmingmodel was developed to simulate hourly operations across all sectors,integrating merit-order dispatch and mass-flow dynamics. Three system configurationswere assessed: (i) a fully coupled system; (ii) a decoupled variant;and (iii) a reference system. Results showed that local municipalitiesand utilities can use sector coupling to balance industrial and district energyneeds, reducing overall system costs and emissions. The fully coupled systemincreased district heating energy efficiency by 7%, resulting in a yearlysavings of 15% in heating costs. The cooling sector demonstrated higher performance,resulting in a 23% reduction in operation cost. Led to a two-foldbenefit of 21 million DKK in revenue from excess heat, 58 million DKK inavoided cooling costs, and 191 million DKK in additional hydrogen sales.
